[2026-10-29 23:59] AI: I've roughly halved the CPU each training game costs and built the multi-machine setup. Everything is on a separate branch, `perf`, in a worktree at `/Users/alon/projects/alpha_heroes/.worktrees/perf`. It's not merged, because joint2 is running on main and another session is working there. All 260 tests pass, and the smoke runs, including a master plus a worker over TCP, trained cleanly. Nothing here changes what is learned or played.

| Battle decision cost on this Mac (CPU ms) | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| building the map | 4.57 | 0.02 |
| VCMI client | 8.01 | 3.85 |
| trainer process | 1.90 | 0.38 |
| model inference on CPU | 12.96 | 9.14 |
| **total** | **27.6** | **13.4** (101 → 178 decisions/s on the same cores) |

With battle inference on the PC's GPU, a battle decision costs a CPU about 4.3 ms.

**Small things with a huge cost (you asked to be told):**
- **A full game-state copy on every decision.** The attack values copied the whole game state through savegame serialization each decision, 37% of a battle client's CPU, more in campaign games. It's now one copy per battle: 6.16 → 2.26 ms of attack-value work per decision on identical battles.
- **A new map-builder process for every generated battle.** That was ~0.2 s of CPU per battle; one persistent builder now does a map in 2–4 ms.
- **zlib level 6 in the map AI's records.** It was ~38% of the map AI's busy CPU, and Python then recompressed every decision. Campaign game CPU dropped 9.5 → 6.0 ms per decision.
- **Battle records sent as int64.** Python scanned every array to narrow it. C++ now sends int32, which the inference link already used.

**GPU training:**
- **Attention trunk.** The relation bias folds exactly into PyTorch's fused attention, so the large bias tensors are never built. Results match to float rounding; it's 2× faster on CPU and −7% per step on the Mac GPU. I expect more on CUDA but couldn't test it.
- **Update inputs** cross to the GPU as int32 (1.9 → 1.0 GB per update).
- **Campaign learner:** one GPU sync per step instead of ~25, and non-blocking input copies on CUDA.
- **Campaign inference** now runs on CUDA when the machine has it; it was hard-wired to the CPU at 5–10 ms per decision.
- I tried `torch.compile` and left it out: its gradients disagreed badly with normal mode in a CPU test, and I have no CUDA access to check it properly.

**Other machines:** a worker runs only the games. Every decision goes to the master's GPU over TCP, about 4 KB compressed. Workers push records and finished campaign games to the master, which tells them when to pause and when its buffer is full. Pushing beats the dataloader asking for games one at a time because nothing waits on a round trip.
```sh
# master (PC)
campaign_model.joint ... --set remote_port=7700
# each worker; copy the master's runtime/remote-token to it first
.venv/bin/python -m battle_model.worker --master <pc address> --machine configs/machines/mac-m4/worker.toml
```
Point workers mostly at campaign games: in joint2 the battle learner waited ~35 s per update for campaign battles. On the PC, WSL2 needs mirrored networking and inbound firewall rules for ports 7700–7760; the README section "On several machines" has the exact commands.

**Found but not mine:** VCMI processes an area attack's targets in memory-address order, so about 1 in 10,000 attack values differ by a few gold between runs. That's probably the ~1% of evals that don't replay exactly. I recommend fixing it (sort targets by unit id); it's a genuine engine bug fix.

**Not tested:** anything CUDA-specific, or the 5090 machine settings I set (campaign inference on 1 process, `micro_batches = 1`). They're marked unmeasured. The worker config for this Mac is an estimate too.

**Decision for you: merging into main.** Old and new code work together in either order, so the merge itself can't break joint2. I recommend merging when you next stop joint2: `git merge perf` from main, `cmake --build build`, then resume. Squash the three work-in-progress commits however you like.

**Possible next steps, each changing model code you own:**
- **Action heads:** the battle model scores all 5,236 melee-from and 13,090 spell-hex entries per decision, though on average only ~3 and ~7 are legal. Scoring only legal entries gives identical outputs for much less work; worth it for CPU inference, less so on the 5090.
- **Campaign features:** the campaign model recomputes its hand-made features three times per update. Separating the parameter-free parts would let them be cached like the battle model's.

My test runs left ~300 MB of checkpoints, which I deleted. The worktree's build (2.9 GB) can go with the worktree after the merge. Measurements and details are in `docs/performance_2026-10-29.md` on the branch.

[2026-10-30 17:39] AI: Short answer: yes and yes. The PC never waits on this Mac, and a worker reconnects by itself. I read this in the code; it has not been tested with a real network drop yet.

**PC side (the master): training continues without the Mac.**
- Nothing on the PC waits for the Mac.
  - The battle learner takes whatever is in its buffer, and the PC's own actors keep filling it.
  - The campaign learner takes any 4 or more finished games, from anyone.
  - Each Mac connection has its own thread on the hub and on the inference servers, so a dead connection blocks only that thread.
- **What is lost:** whatever the Mac had in progress. That means battles and campaign games not yet finished, since a campaign game is sent only once it ends. Everything already received stays in training.
- **What slows:** if most campaign games run on the Mac, the campaign learner updates less often until it returns. So the PC should keep at least 4–8 games of its own, enough for an update without the Mac.

**Mac side (the worker): it rejoins automatically.** Run it without `--once`. On a lost connection it logs "lost the master", stops its games, retries every 10 s, and rejoins as a new worker (`w2-…`) with the current model. Its records are never stale, because every decision uses the PC's current model. It also waits through a restart of the PC's run.

**Three weak spots:**
1. **Silent drops** (Wi-Fi outage, lid closed). With no disconnect signal, the worker waits on a dead connection until TCP gives up, which on the PC takes up to about 15 minutes. If the network returns before that, the connection usually just carries on. Games hung in the meantime are killed after 60 s without output. Adding TCP keepalives to the hub and worker sockets would cut detection to about 30 s; it's a few lines.
2. **The SSH tunnel doesn't restart itself.** If it dies, the worker retries forever against a closed port. Fix: run the tunnel in a restart loop with `ServerAliveInterval=15`. Mirrored networking would remove the tunnel altogether, but needs the WSL restart.
3. **Mac sleep.** Run the worker under `caffeinate -i` so the Mac doesn't sleep under it.

I can add the keepalives and a restarting tunnel script, then test it: a short PC run where I cut the tunnel mid-run and bring it back. That takes about 5 minutes and Zonkey is unaffected.

## Why it isn't built that way

It grew piece by piece, and each piece made sense on the Mac:

- **Battle side:** this already pulls. The generated-battle actors pause while the buffer holds what the next update needs (`actors.py:231`).
- **Campaign side:** this has no throttle. `campaign.games` threads play nonstop, and they only pause during evals (`learner.py:209`). Nothing reads the learner's demand. The learner just drops whatever it can't use.
- **Remote workers:** each worker joins with its own fixed counts (`campaign.games=12`, `generated_actors=2`). I built that part, and that was a mistake.
- **Separate processes:** the campaign update got its own process because of Python's single-thread lock on the Mac. The inference servers got their own processes for the same reason.

On the Mac, the hand-tuned counts happened to match the learner, so only ~20% of games were dropped. On the PC the ratio moved 10× and nothing adjusted. The four separate GPU processes are also what's time-slicing the 5090 under WSL.

## Where I'd change your design

1. **Throttle on the learners' queue of ready data, not on GPU utilization.** "91% busy" at 186 W is exactly the kind of reading that would fool a utilization-based throttle.
2. **Start games ahead of need.** A campaign game takes 1–5 minutes and can only be trained on once it ends. So the number of games in flight has to be about the measured consumption rate times the game length. That should be computed from measurements, not set in a config.
3. **One GPU process trains both models, and inference moves off the GPU.** Inference would run on CPU next to the engines, local or remote. With demand-driven games, we need about 4–5 cores of inference, and the PC has about 10 idle. Then the GPU has one process and nothing to time-slice. A local engine becomes just a worker at 127.0.0.1, the same code as a remote one.
4. **Local first, remote only for the shortfall.** Each host gets slots based on its measured games per hour: add a slot while that keeps rising, stop when it flattens.
5. **One coupling you have to decide.** Campaign games feed both models: their moves go to the campaign learner, their battles to the battle learner. If games are started only for the campaign learner's demand, the campaign-battle share becomes whatever those games produce. That's probably well under your 70%, with generated battles filling the rest. Forcing 70% means playing games whose campaign half gets thrown away, which is what happens now.

## What's unproven

That one GPU process will be much faster is a hypothesis. The evidence so far:
- The battle update took 10.5 s while the campaign learner was idle, against 20.6 s beside it.
- The other AI measured that a forward pass costs 35 ms alone and 200 ms with several processes sharing the GPU.

Before refactoring, I'd time a campaign training step alone on the PC's GPU against one beside the inference servers. That's about 15 minutes, and it needs the GPU free, so after joint5 or with the other AI's OK.

## The change

This rewrites `actors.py`, `learner.py`, `joint.py`, `remote.py` and `worker.py`. Those are the other AI's files, and joint5 runs on them. I'd build it on a branch, test it small on the Mac, and switch the PC over only between runs. The per-machine game and actor counts would come out of the configs.

Two answers from you:
1. Should I build it, coordinating with the other AI?
2. Should the campaign-battle share follow what the campaign's demand produces (my recommendation), or stay a 70% target that plays extra games?

**Is all gameplay going through the loader?** Yes, every game that produces training data does, on both machines:

- Two `IterableDataset`s, generated battles and campaign games, each in a `DataLoader(num_workers=N, batch_size=None, in_order=False)`. N = this machine's ceiling for that kind + workers reserved for remote slots.
- **Each worker process loops:** decide where to play (here, while this machine is under its ceiling and has 3 GB free; else take a remote machine's slot connection; else wait) → run the VCMI game as a subprocess (its decisions go to the inference server over a socket) → turn the records into training arrays in the worker (`battle_examples` + `collate`, numpy) → `yield` the item. A campaign worker yields each battle as it ends, so the battle learner gets them fresh, and then the finished game.
- **The trainer pulls:** one thread per loader takes items only while the learner has room. For generated battles the room is `ahead` (2) updates' worth of their share; when it's full the pull stops, the loader's `prefetch_factor=1` queue fills, and the workers park before their next battle. Campaign games can't pause mid-game, so they're throttled at the start: a worker needs a permit, granted while finished + in-flight decisions are under 2 updates' worth.
- **Remote machines** are plain game servers: 12 connections held open on port 7800; a loader worker takes one, sends the game spec, reads the items back, closes it. So the Mac plays exactly what the PC will train on, and only when the PC's own cores are at their ceiling.
- **The trainer thread** then just assembles an update from the buffered items and trains; the campaign update runs in the same thread between battle updates whenever its games are in.

What's *not* in the loader: the inference server (one separate GPU process for both models, which the measurements forced), and the evaluation games, which run in threads beside training and produce no training data.

[2026-10-31 12:56] USER: what is this inference? why does it take so long?

[2026-10-31 12:57] TOOLS: Bash×2

[2026-10-31 12:57] AI: "Inference" here is the campaign model choosing each move in the self-play games. A game is a VCMI process; every time it is the model's turn to act (move a hero, build, recruit, hire, end the turn) the game client sends the model the current state and waits for the answer. Last night that was about 330 decisions a second across the 24 games, roughly 1,700 decisions a game. Training is the separate thing: the GPU learning from the finished games afterwards.

Why one decision costs 26 ms of a PC core (9 to 12 ms on an M4 core):

- **The input is the whole map, not a summary.** The v2 model embeds every tile of the 36×36 map plus a token for every hero, town and object, so one decision is on the order of 1,500 tokens and about 1.7 MB on the wire, which has to be decompressed and converted before the forward.
- **Batch size is effectively 1.** Each game is a sequential stream: it cannot issue its next decision until the previous one returns. A server can only batch the requests that happen to arrive together from the 24 games, so the CPU runs attention over those 1,500 tokens at tiny batches, where per-call overhead dominates.
- **It runs on CPU, not GPU.** The model itself is small (about 2M parameters by the checkpoint size, dim 64, 2 layers), and a GPU would do a decision in about a millisecond. It is on CPU only because a second GPU process on Windows costs the trainer 40–54% through driver time-slicing. That is the real waste in the setup, and it is why Linux on the PC is the fix that matters.
- **Wi-Fi adds latency.** Each decision to the Mac pays a 14–61 ms round trip. That does not cost cores but it slows every game, so more games are needed in flight to keep the GPU fed, and games are capped by the PC's RAM.

So the cost is not model compute. It is per-decision overhead at batch 1 on CPU cores, forced by the Windows GPU scheduling.

[2026-10-31 13:02] USER: will it be better if inference and data generation happen at the same place for the same games? The Iterable dataset can ask for full records given a game, then we need to have a pool quoue of labeled example, then we can choose batch_size elements at random to pass to the model on the gpu only when the quoue is large enough. The idea here is to have a lot of examples in the quoue from different games OR we can discrad a lot of data and only take few examples from each game so we do not have examples that are so correlated, though this sounds bad I would rather handle correlations well, how did alpha go or other go models did it?

[2026-10-31 13:03] TOOLS: Bash

[2026-10-31 13:03] AI: Two separate questions in there. Short answers, then the Go precedent.

**Same place for inference and games: yes, and it already is where it can be.** The Mac's own slots use the Mac's servers, the PC's battle actors use the PC's CPU servers. The one misplacement is the PC's campaign games asking the Mac over Wi-Fi, 1.7 MB and a 14–61 ms round trip per decision. Co-locating would not make a decision cheaper, it would only remove that latency. The cheap place for the PC's inference is its own GPU, a millisecond a decision, and only the Windows driver's time-slicing stops that. Linux fixes it. Nothing in the data pipeline does.

**A random-sampling example queue: that is a replay buffer, and it changes the algorithm.** The campaign learner is PPO with a clipped importance ratio, which I checked in `campaign_model/train.py`. PPO needs the examples to come from the policy that is being updated, or close to it. Our buffer is already what PPO allows: one update's worth, 32k decisions from 20 to 26 games, shuffled over all decisions before being cut into micro-batches, so a 512 batch holds about 25 decisions from each of the 20 games, two passes with a KL stop. A queue many games deep, sampled uniformly, would feed PPO decisions from policies several versions old. The clip and the KL stop would then throw most of the gradient away. To get a deep buffer you have to pick one of two things:

- Keep PPO and keep the buffer about one update deep, as now. Decorrelation then comes only from games per update, which the PC's RAM caps at about 24.
- Go off-policy on purpose. Either an importance-corrected actor-critic loss (V-trace, as in IMPALA), or targets that do not depend on the acting policy, which is what AlphaZero's losses are. Then the queue can hold hundreds of games and random sampling is exactly right.

**What Go did.** AlphaGo 2016 trained its value net on one position per game from 30 million games, because training on consecutive positions of the same game overfit badly. They could afford to throw away 99% of each game. AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero stopped discarding: they kept the last 500k to 1M games in a replay buffer, sampled positions uniformly across it, and let the buffer's breadth handle correlation. That worked because their targets (the search's move distribution and the final result) are valid for any past policy, and because a batch of 2,048 drawn from 500k games almost never holds two positions from one game. MuZero went further with prioritized replay and reanalysing old games with the current network, which is the same idea as our relabeling of waiting games. None of them trained on-policy.

**My recommendation.** Do not discard data, you are right about that, games are the scarce resource here. Do not put a deep random queue under PPO either, it would silently waste the gradient. If you want the Go-style buffer, the real change is the policy loss: AlphaZero-style targets need a search we do not have, so the realistic path is V-trace with a buffer of a few updates' worth. That is a recipe change for b1 and you to decide, not a pipeline change. The pipeline part you describe, the dataset yielding full games into a pool the trainer samples from, is already how `supply.py` and the learner work, just with the pool one update deep.

[2026-10-31 13:11] USER: so what if instead of learning p(win) or in this case our share of the value, we learn the delta in our share of the value? if some player got a super important artifact at the start they basically get a huge advantage and no one know it so a lot of training examples (from other player) get to learn the their moves are bad without knowing why. If we learn the delta then only the examples of the lucky week are effected. Does that seem right or am I wayyy off, do I have holes in my reasoning? does the math work?

[2026-10-31 13:12] TOOLS: Bash

[2026-10-31 13:12] AI: You are mostly right, and the math works. Two holes, one of them real.

**Why it works.** The policy gradient uses advantage = what happened minus what the value head expected. If the head could see everything, a lucky artifact would already be in its expectation, and nobody's later moves would be blamed. The damage you describe comes only from what the head cannot see: the other player's artifact under fog of war. With a level target, share at day d+k, that hidden fact shifts every later label of every player for the rest of the game, so the head is wrong for the rest of the game and every move of the unlucky players gets a negative advantage. With a delta target, share(d+k) minus share(d), the hidden level cancels. The labeler has the full game record, so it can compute share(d) exactly without the model ever needing to infer it. The targets also telescope: the deltas over a game sum to the end share minus the start share, and the start share is a constant, so maximising deltas is maximising the end share. Nothing is lost in the objective.

**Hole 1, the real one: advantages compound.** An artifact is not a one-time jump in Φ. The stronger hero wins more fights, takes more mines and towns, and the lucky player's share keeps rising week after week. So the other players' deltas stay negative all game, not just in the lucky week. Differencing removes the hidden level, it does not remove the hidden drift. It shrinks the blame from "the whole gap" to "this week's growth of the gap", which is a big improvement, not a cure. The only cure for the drift is the head seeing the cause, meaning features that expose enemy strength as it becomes visible.

**Hole 2, a framing one.** No example "learns its moves are bad" in expectation from a bad baseline alone. A baseline that depends only on the state leaves the gradient unbiased. What a wrong baseline does is add systematic noise, correlated across a whole game, which with 20 games an update is effectively bias. So your conclusion is right, but the mechanism is variance that the update size cannot average out, not a wrong gradient.

**What is already there.** The design has half of this. The growth heads in `labels.py` learn the log of our own empire's value at d+k over its value at the decision: a delta, and of a quantity with no hidden information in it at all. The share heads, which drive the advantage, are still levels. The missing piece is a share-delta target for the advantage: realised share(d+k) minus share(d), against a head predicting that delta. Where the head is already perfect this is identical to today; where share(d) is hidden it strictly removes that error. It is a labels and heads change in Python with a checkpoint migration for the new head, and a recipe decision for you and b1, so I have not touched anything.

If V is the true win probability, the expected change of V between two decisions is zero whatever hidden luck exists. Share of Φ is not: an advantaged player's share is expected to keep rising, so its delta carries hidden drift. That is the whole "compounding" problem in one line, and it tells you what to do with the share.

Suggestions, in the order I would do them:

1. **Keep own growth as the backbone.** The growth heads already learn the log of our own value at d+k over its value now. No hidden information is in that target, and it is already predicted better than the share heads (growth EV 0.33–0.41 against 0.31–0.33 last night). Use its residual as the main advantage term.

2. **Do not gate the share by turn type, attribute it by event.** "Turns where we can affect the enemy" is the wrong unit: the effect of a fight lands days later, and most of an enemy's loss on a given day has nothing to do with us. The labeler has the full ledger, so it can split every change in an enemy's value into what we caused and what we did not. Caused: a battle where our hero was the other side, a town, mine or dwelling of theirs that we took, a hero of theirs we killed. Not caused: their builds, their neutral fights, their artifacts. The interaction term is then the sum of the enemy value changes we caused, in the same log units as growth: minus the log of their total after over before. Killing a hero worth X when the others hold Y gives about X/Y. This is your "share only when we affect the enemy", done by the record rather than by a rule, and the lucky artifact never enters anyone else's label.

3. **Scale both terms into win probability with a calibration curve, not a new head.** Fit, on the games you already have, the end share as a function of current share and days left. Its slope is how much one point of share is worth right now: steep in a close game, flat in a decided one. Multiply the two terms above by that slope. That is the translation you asked for, and it is cheap: a table or a small logistic, refit every few versions. The end head learns the same thing implicitly, and you can read the slope off it once you trust it.

4. **Keep a small end-share term for what attribution misses.** Denial has no event: racing them to a mine, blocking a pass, a scouting hero that makes them retreat. Those show up only as their lower growth, which rule 2 excludes. The existing blend of end credit at a low weight covers this residual, so do not drop it to zero.

The hole to watch: rule 2 can make the model like fights that look good on the ledger and are bad for the game, such as trading a main hero's army for an enemy hero. Rule 1 charges our own loss at full value in the same label, so the sign comes out right as long as the Φ prices are right. That makes `docs/empire_value.md` the place where mistakes would hide, and the war-machine and hero-value decisions already in it the ones to re-read.

All of this is label and advantage code in Python plus a few new progress columns. No model shape change is needed for rules 1 to 4, so no checkpoint migration. It is a recipe change for you and b1, so I have not started it.

[2026-10-31 13:39] AI: **On your two points first.**

Visibility is the right weight, but measure it as the fraction of the enemies' value we can currently see, not the fraction of the map explored. You can know 60% of the map and never have seen their main hero. The labeler has the true ledger and the decision's visible objects, so "seen enemy value over true enemy value" is computable per decision. It belongs on the residual share term, where the hidden-information bias lives, and not on the attributed term, which has no hidden information in it.

The calibration slope is less weird than it sounds: in PPO the advantage is already a detached constant in the policy loss, so multiplying it by a state-dependent positive number is an ordinary per-sample weight, not a second graph. But it is a refinement whose main effect is down-weighting decided games, and it adds an estimation step. Leave it out of this change.

## The change

Replace the share-level targets in the advantage with three terms per decision at day d and horizon k in {2, 5, 7}:

1. **Own growth** G_k = log V_me(d+k) minus log V_me(d). Exists today as the growth labels and heads in `labels.py`. Residual against the growth head.
2. **Attributed interaction** I_k = minus the sum over events in (d, d+k] that we caused of log(enemy total after over before). Caused events: a battle where our hero or garrison was the other side, and an ownership change of their object to us. Their builds, neutral fights and pickups are excluded. Three new heads predict I_k, zero-initialised, which is a checkpoint migration for the model and its snapshots. Residual against the head.
3. **Residual share** R = the existing end-share credit, multiplied by vis(d), the visible fraction of the enemies' value. Weight stays at its current low blend value.

Advantage = the horizon mix of (1) + (2) + (3), capped like the growth labels. The old share heads stay as monitors but leave the advantage. Credit rules, the KL stop, the prepass and the update size are unchanged.

**Step 0, before any training:** a labeler-only script over the saved joint5 games that reports, per decision, I_k's share of nonzero entries, its magnitude against G_k, and the correlation between the old share delta and G_k + I_k. If fewer than about 15% of decisions have a nonzero I_7, the interaction term will be too sparse to matter early and the design should hold the share heads longer.

## Predictions, to be checked against TensorBoard

- **Advantage spread falls.** The per-update `spread` figure in the campaign log (0.02 to 0.06 last night) drops by a third or more within five versions, because the hidden level is gone from the labels. If it does not fall, the hidden-information story is wrong and the change should be reverted.
- **The interaction heads start near zero explained variance and climb slowly.** EV below 0.1 for the first 20 versions, since the target is sparse. Growth EV stays at 0.33 to 0.41. If growth EV falls, the migration broke something.
- **Behaviour shifts toward contact.** Battles against player heroes per game and towns taken from players per game both rise within 30 versions. Eliminations in the eval rise. These are the first signs and should come before any score change.
- **The failure mode to watch is bad trades.** If own value lost in player battles per game rises faster than enemy value destroyed, the Φ prices are rewarding fights the game does not, and the place to look is `docs/empire_value.md`, not the labels.
- **Eval against Nullkiller2** stays flat for the first 20 versions, then improves over the 0.20 plateau by version 50 after the change. Flat or down at version 60 is the revert trigger, with a return to the share-level advantage from the kept heads.

What this will not fix: denial without an event, such as racing to a mine or blocking a pass. That stays inside the residual share term, and the visibility weight will under-credit it early in games. I consider that the right trade until the attributed term is shown to work.

## Where the time goes today

| resource | measured (joint7, PC, this evening) |
|---|---|
| GPU | busy ~60%: an update of 200–260 s every ~380 s, 3 passes over ~60k decisions |

The key finding is what a game waits on. A Nullkiller2-only 4-player game plays a whole turn in ~60 ms of wall time. A training game spends ~70 ms per decision, nearly all of it a round trip to the six CPU inference servers, which run at 100% and cost ~33 ms of CPU per campaign decision. The engine is not slow. The model forward on the CPU is the throttle on games, and the GPU trainer idles 40% waiting for them.

## The bug I fixed

Each VCMI game process ran ~14 Intel TBB worker threads that spin. oneTBB sizes its pool by hardware threads (24 on the PC), and Nullkiller2's parallel loops at every advice request wake them all. On the PC those threads showed 60–100k preemptions per 5 s each, mostly kernel time, about 60% of the games' CPU, roughly 3 of the 12 cores. The Mac sampler agreed: TBB's backoff spin was 40% of busy samples plus ~20% kernel time from it.

The fix is an env var in VCMI's thread-pool sizing (`vcmi/lib/AsyncRunner.h`, labelled, no behaviour change) and `VCMI_MAX_WORKERS=4` exported by the headless launcher. Tested on the Mac with the same Nullkiller2 game twice, 150 s each, both finished cleanly with no stall:

| pool | CPU per turn played | wall per turn |
|---|---|---|
| uncapped (14 threads) | 0.185 s | 60 ms |
| capped at 4 | 0.065 s | 59 ms |

## The extreme options, ranked by gain

1. **Linux on the PC (biggest).** With CUDA graphs, one GPU inference process serves ~800 campaign decisions/s versus ~160/s from six CPU cores today, and the PC's CPU would go entirely to games. Under Windows the WDDM driver time-slices the trainer ~2x when another process uses the GPU, so on Windows this only pays if passes drop 3 to 1. On Linux the trainer keeps most of its speed and the whole CPU budget moves to games. Estimate 3–5x on its own.
2. **RAM to 64 GB.** The PC runs 10 games because loader workers hold 10.9 GB. Doubling RAM takes it to ~30 games; after the TBB fix the CPU can carry that. Estimate 2–3x on games, until the trainer is the limit.
3. **A cheaper decision.** The U-Net plus tile readers are 46% of the forward and the fixed 8 hero windows cost +47% over the ~2.5 real heroes. Options, each roughly 1.3–2x on both inference and training: budget the trainer's windows to the real heroes (keeps the CUDA graphs via a fixed top-k budget with an eager fallback on overflow); stamp heroes onto the map after the U-Net so the map encoding can be cached across the ~18 decisions of a turn; a smaller window or cell width; drop the v1-only inputs that are 43% of every 876 KB record and feed the decode waits.
4. **Trainer side.** Passes 3 to 2 (1.5x per decision, your earlier call), decoding in processes instead of threads (the decode threads starve on the GIL, ~13% of an update), several games per loader process (−6 GB of RAM).

Not levers, measured: CPU batching (15 ms at batch 4 versus 20 ms at batch 1, and servers see ~11 requests/s so batches do not form), more decode threads, bf16, torch.compile.

**WSL is not Linux for this purpose.** CUDA inside WSL2 runs through the Windows WDDM driver (GPU paravirtualization). Every measurement that hurts here was taken under WSL: the trainer losing half its speed beside a second GPU process, the spill into system RAM past 32 GB, the 60% of a core the trainer's main thread spends in kernel calls, the 27 GB RAM cap. "Linux on the PC" means booting Linux natively, a dual boot. The trade is that Windows, and Zonkey's WSL training, are unavailable while Linux runs.

**Item 3 is not a hero limit.** No hero is dropped. The model computes a 33×33 window of (hero, tile) pairs per hero slot. The schema has 8 slots, a player averages 2.5 heroes. CUDA graphs need fixed shapes, so the trainer and the GPU server compute all 8 windows for every decision and zero the 5.5 empty ones. The CPU server skips the empty slots, and that is the 119 vs 175 ms measurement: the empty slots cost 47% of the forward. The fix is a shared budget per micro-batch: 64 decisions have ~160 real heroes, so compute a fixed 320 windows filled with the real heroes first. A decision with 8 heroes borrows from one with 1. Shapes stay fixed, the graph works, and in the rare micro-batch with more than 320 heroes the eager path runs. The window tensors are the biggest in the step, so I expect 25–40% off the GPU step plus memory for larger micro-batches.

The second part of item 3, the per-turn map cache, is different. The U-Net encodes the whole map on every decision, and the ~18 decisions of a turn see nearly the same map. Today heroes are stamped onto the map before the U-Net, with their current movement points, so its input changes every decision. If the stamping moved after the U-Net (heroes already read tiles through the tile reader), the map encoding could be computed once per turn and reused. That block is 46% of the forward. It changes the architecture, so it is your call.

**Item 4, each in a sentence.**
- Passes 3 to 2: every update trains 3 times over the same 60k decisions; 2 passes is a third less GPU time per decision. b1 set 3 when the GPU was idle; it no longer is.
- Decode in processes: the update's inputs are zlib-compressed and 3 threads decompress them ahead of the GPU. The main thread holds Python's lock 90% of the time launching kernels, the decoders starve, and the GPU waits ~30 s of every 230 s update. Processes have no shared lock.
- Several games per loader process: each in-flight game is its own Python process of 340–830 MB (torch loaded, fork pages copied), 10.9 GB in all. Three games per process would free ~6 GB, room for ~9 more PC games under the RAM cap.

[2026-11-03 07:30] AI: No. A custom CUDA kernel does not touch the bottleneck, and the part it could touch has a small ceiling.

**The wall is CPU inference for the games, not the GPU.** Games produce ~570k decisions an hour and the trainer consumes exactly that much. The update takes ~230 s of a ~380 s cycle, and the trainer idles the rest waiting for games. A faster GPU step would lengthen the idle time, not add a game. Under Windows the GPU cannot take the inference load without the 2x hit on the trainer, so freed GPU time has nowhere useful to go.

**Even on the GPU step, the model is too small for kernels to matter much.** The map is 2×36×36 cells, the windows 33×33, the tile attention 51×2592, batch 64. At those sizes each kernel runs a few microseconds, so the step is launch-bound, and the StepGraph CUDA graphs already remove the launch cost. Fusing elementwise ops would cut maybe a third to a half of the step. There is no big memory-bound or compute-bound op where hand-written code beats cuDNN or cuBLAS by a large factor. The one CPU hotspot, convolution_backward at 15%, is already oneDNN.

**The cheap version of the same idea** is torch.compile, which writes those fused kernels for you. It fails on the model at encoders.py:321. Fixing that costs an hour, not a week, and is the right first move once the trainer becomes the wall, which happens after Linux or more RAM makes games 2–3x faster.

**One GPU idea worth measuring before any kernel work:** b1's 2x penalty was measured for a second GPU process. Streams inside one process are not time-sliced by WDDM. Serving inference from inside the trainer process on a side stream could give games GPU inference under Windows. The risk is Python's lock, since the trainer's main thread holds it ~90% of the time, so the serving thread would need to be C++ or very thin. That is a b1 design question. I can ask whether it was already tried and rejected.

[2026-11-03 09:46] AI: **Short answer on the Grail:** never, for three independent reasons. The puzzle map is not an input, there is no DIG action, and the memory is not trained at all in joint7. On that last point: PPO feeds the recorded `mem` back as an input and no loss touches the memory output, so the writer gets no gradient. Truncated BPTT exists only in imitate.py, which joint7 does not run (NK2's advice is a KL teacher, not an imitation stream). The writer is a near-zero random projection of the previous decision, so nothing survives a turn boundary. That makes item 1 below the biggest "never" in the current run.

Ranked by how often the situation comes up in today's games (36×36, 2–4 players, water at random, 28–112 days):

1. **Anything that needs remembering** (every decision). An enemy hero that steps off revealed tiles is gone from the inputs that instant; where it was heading, which part of the map a scout already checked, what a sign or a visited hut said, a plan spanning turns: none of it can be kept. The memory exists in the contract but is untrained. Fix: BPTT in PPO (the known to-do), or cheaper, auxiliary losses on the memory output (predict the last-seen enemy positions, the days since each town was seen).

2. **Arranging one army** (NK2's most common non-move request, 1,532 per 400 turns). ARMY needs two different holders; the encoder skips from == to. A hero can never split a stack into more slots or merge, and there is no disband. A 2-stack army fights every battle as 2 stacks, so the battle model never gets blockers or a 7-slot layout unless the campaign model stumbled into it. Fix: allow from == to with the HALF/ONE amounts into an empty slot, plus a DISBAND entry.

3. **Artifacts** (every game; NK2 67 exchanges per 400 turns). VCMI puts a pickup into the first free slot, else the backpack. No action equips, swaps or hands an artifact to another hero. The first ring found is worn forever; every better one sits in the backpack; the scout who found the sword can never give it to the main hero; combination artifacts never assemble. Fix: an ARTIFACT action (hero, backpack index → slot; and at EXCHANGE, to the other hero).

4. **Buying the basic creature when the upgraded one is on sale.** The recruit mask carries `ids.back()`, the best creature per level, so once an upgraded dwelling stands only the dear one is for sale. Same at external dwellings: the C++ picks "the dearest creature on offer" and the model picks only the amount, which also violates "Python owns the science". Fix: a basic/upgraded bit on RECRUIT; the dwelling's creatures as options.

5. **Quests and guarded rewards: the terms are hidden.** Seer's Huts and Quest Guards ask a refusable yes/no with the reward as components (CQuest.cpp sets canRefuse); the "attack the guards?" question of guarded reward objects lists the guards the same way. Our yes/no encoding keeps the object type, the first number of the text and the sound, and drops the components. The model can never weigh a quest's reward against its price or a guard list beyond the object type's average. Fix: encode the components onto the YES option (o_type, o_subtype, o_amount already exist).

6. **Town spells.** A town's mage guild contents are not an input; t_built gives only the guild level and h_spells only what our heroes already learned. The model can never plan "go learn Town Portal in that town". Fix: t_spells (8 towns × 70 bits).

7. **A hero in the garrison slot** (NK2 228 per 400 turns). No action moves a hero into or out of a town's garrison, so a town holds one hero inside at a time: a second hero cannot enter to recruit or learn while the first stays, and the garrison-plus-visitor defence is impossible.

8. **Water.** No shipyard or BuildBoat action, Scuttle Boat untargeted, only Summon Boat or a boat already ashore. Mines, towns and rivals across water are unreachable, so such a game cannot be won. How often the generator makes islands at 36×36 I have not measured.

9. **Hard limits in the contract.** Maps above 36×36 (MAP_TILES), more than 8 rival heroes or 8 rival towns in view (the farthest vanish), more than 8 options (Town Portal with 9+ towns), the backpack past 8, map taverns (closed unasked), DISMISS (reserved), thieves' guild information (nothing). All fine for the current maps.

10. **What the reward cannot see** is hard rather than never: Φ holds no term for position, threat or exploration by walking, so defensive placement and scouting are learnable only through the end-of-game share, a weak signal in 28–112-day games that mostly end at the cap.

Items 2, 4, 5 and 6 are contract additions of a few mask entries or input fields each. Items 1 and 3 are the ones that change what the model is.

Every question kind goes through one shared head: yes/no, select, level-up, pick-an-object, and the dwelling amount.

Your direction is right, with four changes. Learned embeddings plus a match score fixes the cause of today's failure, not just the symptoms.

Why the current head fails

The YES token is the same vector for every yes/no question. The question's identity (a quest guard? a dwelling?) lives only inside the global token. The query alone must therefore separate "YES at a border guard" from "YES at a Crypt", and the one learned direction for YES drifted into a NO lean everywhere.

What I'd build

1. The decision state (your "last hidden state"): one small SwiGLU over what we already have, the global token and the asked hero's token after the second pass. Not a new trunk pass. Cosine scoring needs a nonzero, nonlinear query, and these tokens are shared with MOVE, so it's worth one cheap layer of its own.
2. Every option gets an identity key, built from embedding tables the model already trains elsewhere (weight tying):
   - Skill (level-up, University): the hero encoder's (skill, level) row, the same vector that means "this hero has Wisdom". Every hero that has Wisdom trains the key that offers Wisdom.
   - Creature (dwelling amounts, joins): the army encoder's creature row.
   - Yes/no YES: "act on this object", from the asked object's (type, subtype) embedding. YES at a Quest Guard and YES at a Crypt become different keys, from inputs we already have, so no C++ is needed for existing questions.
   - NO: a "decline" key, plus the schema-11 consequence flags (refusing a join means a battle).
   - Components (School of War: attack or defence; chests: gold or experience): the existing per-component table. Amounts and costs stay small scalar features on the key.

   Options stay transformer tokens, so the state still sees what's on offer. The contextualized token adds onto the key through a zero-init residual, so each key starts as a pure identity and learns to use context only if that helps.
3. Score: logit_i = atanh(0.995 · cos(h, key_i)) + prior_i, softmax over the options.
   - Random init gives cos ≈ 0, so every question starts near uniform.
   - The 0.995 keeps atanh finite: each logit is within ±3.0, so two options can reach about 0.997.
   - Priors add outside the atanh.
4. Expert knowledge out of the forward: domain_knowledge calls one option_priors(x, f), which calls one function per rule:
   - NK2's skill scores (level-up and University);
   - the battle and join priors;
   - NK2's YES at dwellings, guards and quests.

Per hour the policy now moves roughly a thousand times less than in the run that learned. PPO's clipping never engages and the KL control can only lower the rate further. The eval spread of ±0.004 across 1,087 updates is what a frozen policy looks like, not a plateau of a trained one. **Why the gradient is mostly noise, so even more steps would help less than they should**

- **The data is 60% lopsided campaign battles.** In the last epochs the attacker won 84% and the defender retreated in 70 to 85% of its battles. The outcome of those fights is set by the armies, not by the actions, so their advantages carry no information. The example weight already drops them to as little as 0.05, which means the 60% real share mostly dilutes the batch. - **Credit is 85% a two-round window.** outcome_share sits at its floor of 0.15 for the whole run because the value EV is above 0.4. Anything that pays off beyond two rounds (positioning, waiting, keeping shooters covered) gets almost no credit.

[2026-11-05 15:31] AI: **How the loss is computed for a MULTI decision**

Two parts, both per decision. The C++ making several engine requests changes nothing in the loss.

- **PPO part:** the chosen action's log-probability is log p(type = MULTI) + log p(entry | MULTI) from the multi table, times the horizon advantage, clipped. Same as any other type.
- **Teacher part:** on 90 to 95% of turn and exchange decisions, at weight 1.6 to 1.8 right now, the loss is −log( p(NK2's label) + Σ p(accepted entries) ). A MULTI entry only ever enters through the accept set: RECRUIT_ALL and RECRUIT_ALL_HERO when NK2's first request is a recruit in that town, GATHER wherever it is legal, GIVE_ALL when NK2's best army is not yet on the receiver. When NK2's request has no match of ours (3.8% of advice: boats, garrison swaps, dismissals, within-army arranging, teleport steps), there is no label, and the loss falls on the accept set alone, or on nothing.

**Is it right?** The form is right when every member of the set is equally acceptable. Three things are wrong around it:

1. The set's breadth is the whole lever. GATHER accepted everywhere legal switches the teacher off on those decisions, which is how the towns emptied. RECRUIT_ALL accepted only when NK2's first request is that recruit is the opposite extreme.
2. The gradient inside the log-sum goes to the member the model already favours, so an accepted entry the model likes absorbs the whole label. That is the rich-get-richer path GATHER took.
3. The label is NK2's first request only. Anything it would do later in the same turn but has not named yet is penalised at this decision. That breaks your rule that order inside a turn must not matter. The pending set only catches what NK2 named earlier.

**Decisions NK2 cannot make: yes, we take loss on them, and it has already done its damage.** The cross-entropy normalises over every legal entry, so each advised decision pushes down everything NK2 cannot express, with NK2's inability read as a judgement. The run's own action shares:

| our action share | early joint7 | now |
|---|---|---|
| CAST (NK2 casts no adventure spells; ours was ~16% of turn decisions on 2026-10-31) | 0.001 | 0.00005 |
| ARTIFACT (NK2 equips, but never in a form we match) | 0.008 | 0.00003 |
| MULTI (77 updates in) | 0.10 | 0.03 |

Town Portal, Dimension Door and Fly are at one cast per ten thousand decisions. The campaign model has unlearned adventure magic and artifact handling because its teacher cannot do them. MULTI is on the same path, with b1's costs pushing in the same direction.

**What should happen instead:** the teacher should only judge among actions it can express. Condition the cross-entropy on that support: log p(label) − log Σ p(type) over the expressible types, so CAST, ARTIFACT, DISMISS and any MULTI entry not in the accept set drop out of the normaliser. The teacher then says nothing about them and PPO decides. This is a type-level renormalisation in train.py where chosen_logp and entries_logp read type_logp. The within-table distributions stay as they are.

Two refinements of the same idea:

- For your order rule, restrict further by family. A MOVE or TRAVEL label normalises over hero actions plus END. A town label normalises over town actions plus END. END stays everywhere because "nothing more worth doing" is a judgement NK2 can make. The pending set becomes unnecessary.
- In exchanges, normalise over ARMY, GIVE_ALL and END only, so GIVE and EQUIP are no longer punished by every troop-move label.

When the request is unmatched, skip the teacher loss for that decision rather than teaching a substitute from the plan.

Add one metric with it: the share of the teacher's probability mass that falls on inexpressible types per update. Today that number would have shown the CAST collapse within a day. And A/B it like the other label changes. The 2026-11-05 collapse came from a label change that looked harmless.

**What happened at 1138** (TensorBoard campaign run and the trainer log)

| | v1128–1133 | v1138–1145 (peak) | v1240 (now) |
|---|---|---|---|
| eval/campaign_value_loss | 0.0004–0.0006 | 0.0081–0.0104 | 0.0026 |

| target std, V_end | 0.098 | 0.155 | 0.12 |

| explained variance, V_end | 0.34 | 0.21 | 0.23 |
| loss weight of the value term | 356 | 146 | 254 |
| credit trust in V | 0.33–0.47 | 0.17 | 0.29 |

**Why it is higher: the task did get harder, and the labels moved under the heads.** The label spread grew 2.4× in standard deviation at the peak, about 6× in variance, and it is still 1.6× what it was. That is not the Φ unit alone. It is the policy's own churn after schema 14: give-alls sending armies back the same day, towns emptied and lost, eliminations 19 to 28 of 48. Each of those swings the shares and the day's growth, so the targets became volatile. On top of that the Φ unit, the spellbook factor and the meeting value shifted every label, so all seven heads mispredicted at once. The eval loss is the excess over label entropy, and it rose 25× against a 6× variance rise, so the fit got worse too, which the explained variances confirm.

**Why it is not back.** Three throttles, all of them by design and all of them wrong for this situation:

1. The loss-share balancer cut the value weight from 356 to 146 exactly when the heads were most wrong. It holds each term at a fixed share of the policy's shared gradient, so when the value gradient grew (its actual share hit 0.33 to 0.47 against a target of 0.15), the balancer pushed it back down. A head that suddenly needs re-fitting gets throttled at that moment.
2. The head variance weighting divides by target variance. When the share heads' variance tripled, their weights fell from about 8.6 to 5.3, again when they most needed gradient.
3. LR 1e-5 constant, and the value readouts are tiny (rms 0.006 to 0.012). A re-fit to shifted labels takes hundreds of updates at that pace. It is 100 updates in and the growth heads have recovered half the lost explained variance.

The cost is not only the value loss. Trust in V fell from 0.47 to 0.17, so the credit went MC-heavy and the policy gradient has been noisier for a hundred updates. A Φ change buys a hundred updates of degraded learning.

**The gradient norm.** Pre-clip total is 8 to 16 now, 11 to 19 before the jump, 37 at version 97, with grad_clip at 0.5. So it is clipped about 20× at every step and has been all run. Not larger now. With Adam a constant clip ratio is nearly a no-op, so it is not the cause, but it also means the clip is not acting as a spike guard, only as a rescale. The shared-layer gradients per term are small (teacher 0.4, policy 0.15, value 0.07). The total lives in the heads' own parameters, which the value weight of several hundred inflates, and which Adam normalises per parameter anyway.

**Suggestions.** Stop changing Φ for a while. Each change costs about a hundred updates of value fit and credit quality, and there were four Φ edits in three days. When a label change is deployed, exempt the value term from the balancer's cap for 20 to 30 updates so its weight can rise with its gradient instead of being cut. Give the value readouts the ×10 gain that was offered on 2026-11-02, or a separate learning rate; at 1e-5 they cannot follow a shifted target. The clip is a separate, smaller point: raise it toward the typical norm so it only catches spikes.

[2026-11-05 18:58] AI: Short answers: a HotA AI plugin is technically possible but a reverse-engineering project, not an interface; and no, there are no ranked-game replays to learn from.

**An AI plugin for HotA**

- HotA has no AI interface. HotA and the HD mod are closed binary patches on h3hota.exe. The only extension point is the HD mod's plugin loader: a DLL that hooks game functions by memory address, as HotA itself does. The open-source NH3API library documents that pattern (a patcher instance, a hook at an address, the original callable through it).
- A plugin that replaces the AI would hook the adventure-turn and battle-action entry points of the original engine's AI, read the game state from the game's own structures, and call our model through ONNX. Every piece of that has to be reverse-engineered from a specific h3hota.exe, breaks on every HotA release (1.8.0 Dec 2025, 1.8.1 Aug 2026), is Windows-only, and depends on the HotA Crew's tolerance. Nobody has published such a plugin.
- The engine semantics would differ from VCMI's: our C++ encoder, the fingerprint logic and the action execution all speak VCMI's callback API. A HotA plugin means a second encoder against undocumented structures. I would call it a 2 to 4 month effort for a strong reverse engineer, with no guarantee the HotA Crew does not break it on purpose.
- The realistic route stays VCMI's HotA mod. If VCMI finishes HotA, the AI reaches HotA players without touching HotA.

**Ranked games as training data: no.**

- HotA has no replay format and the lobby stores none. HotA Meta tracks ranked results: template, factions, heroes, outcome, about 5.4M games. That is win-rate statistics, not decisions.
- So there is nothing to imitate at the decision level. What those statistics could give us is priors: hero and faction strength by template, typical game length. Useful for Φ's hero and creature values, not as trajectories.
- Human decision data for Heroes 3 does not exist anywhere in bulk. Nullkiller2 stays the only teacher, and self-play the only source of trajectories.

Sources: [NH3API modding library](https://verifico.duckdns.org/void2012/NH3API), [HD mod on Nexus](https://www.nexusmods.com/heroesofmightandmagiciii/mods/3), [HotA Meta dashboard](https://hotameta.com/), [h3hota.com](https://h3hota.com), [HotA on GOG](https://www.gog.com/en/game/heroes_of_might_and_magic_iii_horn_of_the_abyss)

[2026-11-06 07:57] AI: Short answer: Adam is not the problem, the plumbing around it is. Both of your points are right in mechanism, and the measurements say where exactly.

**What Adam does with noise.** Per parameter the step is lr × m̂/√v̂. For a parameter whose gradient is mostly noise, m̂/√v̂ is a random number of fixed size, about √((1−β1)/(1+β1)) = 0.23 at β1 0.9, so the parameter random-walks at 0.23·lr per step no matter how weak its signal is. SGD would shrink that step with the gradient; Adam normalises it away. Our signal ratio (median |m̂|/√v̂) is 0.17 to 0.26 on the campaign side and 0.12 to 0.26 on the battle side, so most parameters live in that regime: three quarters of every step is noise, at full size. Two consequences you may not have in mind:

- Loss weights do nothing for a head's own parameters under Adam. The value term's weight of 350 changes only the shared trunk's gradient mix; the value readouts move at lr regardless. Weighting is a trunk-only knob.
- Balancing by gradient norm (the loss shares) treats noise as signal. A term whose gradient is mostly noise has a large norm from the noise, and GradNorm gives it the same influence on the trunk as a clean term. Our measured gradient noise scales (the batch at which a term's noise equals its signal, `campaign_noise/*`) say the value terms are signal-dominated at the 4,096-decision step (noise scales 5 to 700 decisions) while the policy term's noise scale is 300 to 6,000 and often unmeasurable. So the norm balance hands the trunk 20% of a mostly-noise policy gradient and 60% teacher, and squeezes the one term with clean signal to 15%. Your point 1 is right about the mechanism; the noisiest term on the trunk is the policy, not the long horizons, whose labels are noisy but whose gradients at 4k decisions still carry signal.

**Derived losses.** The advantage is computed from the critic (V7 as baseline, trust-mixed with MC), and the critic's labels come from the policy's own play. Theory is unambiguous here: two-timescale actor-critic (Konda and Tsitsiklis, Borkar) needs the critic on the faster timescale, with a step ratio critic/actor that grows, so the actor sees a converged critic. We run the opposite: one LR for both, the critic at 15% of the trunk's gradient, the trunk shaped 60% by an exogenous teacher, and the actor's KL budget inflated to 0.015 × (1 + 0.6/0.2) = 0.06 by the teacher's share. The actor moves 2 to 4× faster than designed, the critic's targets move with it, the critic lags, trust falls (0.40 to 0.25), the credit falls back to MC, the actor's gradient gets noisier. That is the loop we measured yesterday, and it is a direct consequence of the timescale ordering. The trust mechanism is a third coupling: a controller on the critic's EV with a 10-update pooling lag, next to the GradNorm controller with a 10-update EMA and the KL controller. Three loops at the same time constant hunt.

**What to do, in order of leverage**

1. Critic faster than actor. Separate parameter group for the value heads at 10× the policy's LR, or value pre-passes each update with the policy loss off, or a critic branch off the detached trunk plus the Φ features with its own optimizer. The last one also frees the critic from the teacher's 60% ownership of the trunk. This is Phasic Policy Gradient's reason to exist. A critic LR above your cap is your decision; the cap was made for the policy.
2. Remove the KL inflation: the KL target is the policy's movement whoever caused it. Back to 0.015.
3. Weight the trunk's terms by signal, not norm: fixed weights from the measured noise scales, re-measured only at deploys. Delete the ×1.25-per-update controller. Keep KL control as the one remaining loop.
4. Replace trust-by-EV with a fixed bias-variance blend (a λ), or a slow floored EMA. The TD/MC mix is a design choice, not a feedback variable.
5. Longer momentum where the signal ratio says noise: β1 0.95 to 0.99 for the trunk shrinks the noise step by √2 to √10 (0.23σ at 0.9, 0.07σ at 0.99) while the KL control bounds the policy. Equivalent alternative: larger steps.
6. Heads weighted by inverse residual variance (what the "unexplained" metric measures per head), or learned heteroscedastic weights (Kendall and Gal). That replaces head_scale's 1/label-variance, which weights by spread, not by learnable signal.
7. Clip at about twice the typical norm (20) so it catches spikes instead of rescaling every step 20×.

**The theoretical answer**, stated once: a two-timescale actor-critic whose critic does not share the actor's bottleneck, a fixed λ for the TD/MC blend, loss weights set by signal-to-noise or learned uncertainty rather than gradient norms, Adam with momentum matched to the measured signal ratio, and one controller. Nothing exotic, and no different optimizer family would fix a controller stack.

**Head width versus learning rate.** They change different quantities. A higher learning rate changes how fast the critic's function tracks a moving target. A wider head changes which functions it can express, and it also raises its speed, but uncontrollably (more parameters each moving at lr). The two-timescale theorems care only about speed: the critic must converge faster than the actor moves. So the question is which of the two is our deficit, and the code answers it: the campaign critic already has a 128-wide GELU hidden layer over the global token, our heroes' and towns' mean, our player token and the Φ features, with zero-init linear heads on top. If the trunk's features turn out to be the limit (they are 60% the teacher's), the fix is a critic branch reading the detached trunk plus Φ with its own block, not a wider readout.

**The clip.** You are right and I was wrong to say 20. With Adam a clip that binds on every step is a per-step normalisation of the gradient: Adam is invariant to a constant gradient scale, so normalising costs nothing and it damps spikes across steps, which is what you use clipping for. What is wrong is not the value 0.5 but what the norm is made of. The total of about 10 does not come from the trunk, whose per-term shared gradients are 0.07 to 0.4. It comes from two groups scaled up by design: the prior corrections, whose `bounded()` multiplies the raw parameter by CORRECTION_STEP 10 so their gradients are 10× a plain weight's, and the value heads' private parameters, which see the loss at the balancer's weight of about 350. So a spike in a batch's value error shrinks the trunk's gradient for that step by the same factor. That is your hand-crafted-features hypothesis, and it is testable in one update. The fix is to clip per parameter group, each at its own typical norm, which keeps the normalising behaviour and stops one group's spike starving another. Step 0 of the doc measures the group norms; nothing is changed until the numbers are in.

[2026-11-06 17:15] AI: Found it in the paper's own text. Writing the answer now.

**Scatter connections are the step that puts each unit's transformer embedding onto the spatial map at the unit's (x, y), so the convolutional spatial encoder sees per-unit features in place.** The Nature paper never defines the term in its main text; the definition is in the supplementary architecture file: each entity embedding goes through a 1D convolution to 32 channels and a ReLU, then is "scattered into a map layer so that the size 32 vector at a specific location corresponds to the units placed there." That layer is concatenated with the minimap planes and fed to the ResNet spatial encoder. Mechanically it is a scatter into a zero tensor of shape (channels, H, W) at each unit's flat index; implementations differ on collisions, overwrite or add.

Why it matters: before it, the two halves of the encoder were blind to each other. The transformer over units knew each unit's attributes and coordinates but had no map context, and the ResNet knew terrain, creep and visibility but only coarse unit planes. Scattering fuses them in the direction set to grid, so convolutions can reason about local configurations, and the spatial output that feeds the target-location heads becomes unit-aware.

On the number. Fig. 3F is a cumulative ladder, not a one-at-a-time ablation. It measures supervised agents only (imitation of human replays, Protoss vs All) by win rate against the built-in Elite bot:

| Architecture | Win rate vs Elite bot |
|---|---|
| Baseline | 0% |
| + Action delays | 7% |
| + Pointer network | 36% |
| + Transformer | 71% |
| + Scatter connections | 87% |

So the 16 points are the marginal gain of scatter connections on top of the transformer and pointer network, for an imitation agent, not for the RL agent. The paper's Methods adds that architecture components were "chosen and tuned with respect to their performance in supervised learning." The separate 87% to 96% figure in the paper is a different comparison, camera versus non-camera interface.

For our models the analog is placing the stack or hero token embeddings onto the hex grid or map tiles before any spatial layer, rather than giving tokens coordinates as features alone. I have not checked whether either of our encoders already does this.

[2026-11-06 17:30] AI: Both papers checked against the code and the live run. **One trick stands out as directly applicable and large, two more are cheap, and most of the rest we already match or cannot afford.**

## Take

1. **A critic that sees the hidden state.** AlphaStar fed the opponent's observations to its value functions, training only, and it was the biggest RL effect in the paper: the best-response win rate went from 22% to 82%. OpenAI Five did not do this and names it as the promising direction. Our campaign critic reads only our own player's token, our heroes' mean, the global vector and Φ, and the player tokens are built from the heroes and towns we see. Yet the labels are future Φ shares, which depend mostly on what the other players hold, and the trainer already has every player's true Φ from the ledger. Feed the other players' true Φ components into `value_hidden` alone, zero-initialised, never into the policy. This is standard asymmetric actor-critic and stays unbiased because the baseline cannot depend on the action. Before touching the model, bound the gain offline: regress the labels on our features with and without the opponents' truth on recorded games. If the explained variance barely moves, the residual is not hidden information and this is not worth a deploy.

2. **Past versions as opponents, with a forgetting metric first.** AlphaStar's naive self-play reached high Elo but forgot; OpenAI Five played 20% of games against snapshots sampled by a quality score to avoid strategy collapse. Our battle league already does 85% self and 15% past versions. The campaign plays only the current model against itself. Our eval swings between 0.36 and 0.48 are consistent with noise and with cycling, and nothing measures which. Add AlphaStar's forgetting metric, the win rate against our own snapshots from 200 updates back, before adding snapshot opponents. The inference server already serves named snapshots for battles, so the mechanism exists. This stays inside the self-play rule: past versions of ourselves are not NK2.

3. **The Rerun lesson for joint8.** OpenAI Five's from-scratch rerun with the final code took about 20% of the compute and beat the surgered run with over 98% win rate; the surgered model plateaued lower. joint7 has lived through label changes, rollbacks and migrations, which is exactly their surgery. When the fixes settle, start joint8 from scratch and judge it against joint7 at equal compute rather than continuing joint7 by default. Smaller item from the same place: they ran lr 0 for hours after each surgery so Adam's moments could settle; a short lr warm-up after a deploy that changes labels is cheap.

4. **Credit tricks.** Team spirit: OpenAI Five started each hero at 70% local reward and annealed toward team reward, because local reward cuts gradient variance early. Our attributed credit is the local signal; while trust is low, weight it more and let the schedule, not a fixed constant, decide. UPGO: bootstrap from V when the taken action's outcome fell below V, so a lost battle does not punish every decision in it; it added 9 points on top of TD(λ) in their ablation and fits the battle's noisy terminal credit. Time weighting: their shaped reward decayed by 0.6 per 10 minutes so the terminal outcome dominates late; our V_end credit weight is a constant 0.20 at every day.

5. **Entropy.** Both systems kept an entropy bonus; OpenAI Five's ablation found 0.01 best and 0 worse though not fatal. Our battle policy has no entropy term since b1 rejected the floor. Its entropy reads 0.88 to 0.93 now, so no action yet, but if it trends down with flat evals the bonus is the standard answer.

## Already matched

- Architecture: entity tokens with attention, autoregressive type then target, shared unit embeddings carried to the heads. Scatter connections need a spatial stream we do not have. No architecture change recommended.
- Data quality: OpenAI Five found staleness of 8 versions a significant slowdown and targeted 0 to 1; ours is about 1. They found sample reuse of 2 to 3 halves speed in a compute-rich regime; our 2 passes are a data-limited trade and defensible, 4 would not be.
- Optimizer: Adam at 5e-5 falling to 5e-6 on million-timestep batches, PPO clip 0.2, advantage normalisation by running std, rewards zero-sum. Our 1e-5 at 4k decisions sits where their scaling points.
- Exploration by randomising the environment, including making a hard sub-task sometimes easy, is what our generator and random maps do. Scripted macro actions are our MULTI kinds.

## Not for us now

League exploiters, z-statistics with pseudo-rewards, and V-trace are built for a league of many learners on thousands of accelerators. The KL to a frozen supervised policy is worth one thought: AlphaStar's anchor was a small regulariser to a fixed policy, and RL could leave it where leaving paid. Our teacher is 60% of the loss toward NK2's live advice, which caps us at NK2 wherever NK2 is wrong. That is the user's deliberate design, so I note the difference rather than propose a change.

Aside from the run: 90 updates after the optimizer deploy, V7 explained variance is 0.21 to 0.22 from 0.15 and growth 7 is 0.36 to 0.37 from 0.29, trust holds 0.40, and the KL target reads 0.030, not the plan's 0.015.

[2026-11-08 08:41] AI: **Keep the whole-map grid at a fixed 36×36 blocks per level and let the block size grow with the map.** That is the right design for your goal. The model's math is already size-agnostic; the one hard limit is the contract's 36-tile grid, and the trap is fixed-shape batching. With blocks, a 144×144 map is 4 tiles per block, a 36×36 map is 1 tile per block and runs bit-identically to today, and every decision costs the same at every size. The wire, the records, the server, the trainer's batching and the CUDA graphs do not change at all. The alternative the v2 draft envisioned, a true-size tile grid, costs roughly 6× per XL decision and a lot of plumbing. Build the block design first, measure on XL evals, and move to a finer grid only if the coarse far view shows up as a weakness.

## What scales with map size today

I measured the contract and the model at the run's sizes. Only the eight whole-map tile arrays grow with the map. Everything else is already fixed: the eight hero windows of 33×33 tiles, the 8,192-slot object list, the per-block counts, the 18×18 TRAVEL areas and the entity tokens.

| Where | Today at 36×36 | At 144×144 if the grid were tile-exact |
|---|---|---|
| Wire per decision | 259k scalars, tiles 8% | tiles ×16, the wire 2.2× |
| Forward, map-bound share | U-Net 19%, tile reader 16%, tile encoder 2% | that 37% alone becomes ~6× today's whole forward |
| Tile reader memory per decision | ~3 MB | ~45 MB |

The forward shares are a CPU proxy from the Mac; on the GPU the convolution and attention parts are relatively cheaper, so the XL factor would be smaller but still several-fold. The live update spends 193 of 230 s in the graphed GPU steps and 1 s waiting for decode, so the GPU step is what any growth hits.

Raising the tile constant to 144 is the wrong move: every small-map decision would carry 16× the tiles as padding, the U-Net and the tile reader would work on nothing, and because the graphs fix shapes, every batch would be XL-shaped. That is exactly the "small maps super slow" outcome.

## Changes for the block design

- **Engine, labeled and data-side.** The encoder writes the whole-map arrays per block, with the block side computed as the per-block counts already compute it. Per block: flags OR'ed, the majority terrain, a road if any, the top visitable object by a fixed priority, its owner and subtype, the strongest monster and its count. Remove the error for maps wider than 36. Positions stay in tiles everywhere.
- **Model.** Derive the block side per decision from the map-size input. Divide positions by it where heroes and towns are stamped onto the grid and where window tiles are mapped to grid cells. Multiply block offsets by it before the distance buckets, so the bias stays in tiles. Average the reach scatter per block instead of summing, since several window tiles now land in one block. Add the scale as an input to the tile encoder and the global token through a zero-init added input, so current checkpoints load unchanged.
- **MOVE stays tile-exact.** The per-window tile facts, the object gold, the fight estimates and the MOVE prior, currently gather from the shared grid. On big maps a block's top object is wrong for 15 of its 16 tiles, so compute those facts from the window arrays, which are tile-exact at any size and already on the wire. The U-Net's output still gives each window tile its block's learned context.
- **Unchanged.** The U-Net, the tile reader, TRAVEL, the per-block counts, the contract layout, the record format, the server and the step graphs.
- **Test.** Side 1 must reproduce today's outputs bit for bit, and a synthetic 144×144 input must run through the forward at the same shapes.

Changes needed whichever design you pick:

- Map sizes in the config, and per-size game time limits and day caps. A 56-day small-map game takes about 200 s; an XL game would hit the 2,400 s limit and be killed, its records never trained on.
- A controlled share of big games per update. Games are the wall, and one XL game yields thousands of decisions while taking many times longer, so an uncontrolled mix swings both the update size and the data rate.
- XL maps in the eval set and per-size eval columns. A mixed mean hides a regression on either size.
- The MOVE window radius of 16 misses same-day road moves beyond it on big maps. TRAVEL covers them at 8×8-tile areas on XL. Keep it and measure before widening the window, which costs per window tile.

## The true-size alternative, for comparison

Size classes of 36, 72, 108 and 144: a contract per class, the record length naming the class as it already names older schemas, minibatches bucketed by class with a tile budget so that rows times tiles stays constant, the grid side read from the batch, adaptive pooling of the half-resolution level to the 18×18 TRAVEL grid, a deeper U-Net or global pooling so XL maps still get whole-map context, per-class graphs on the trainer and per-class families on the server, and the encoder writing the map at its real size. Small maps stay at today's cost, an XL decision costs about 6× and 15× the tile memory, and the transfer story is worse: today's U-Net sees the whole map at its bottom level, and at 144 it would not. Its one advantage is tile-exact objects far from any hero. If the block design's XL play shows it ignoring far objects it could see, a 72-block class is the middle step, with two classes to plumb instead of four.

[2026-11-08 09:03] AI: The plan is written to `docs/map_size_plan.md`, uncommitted like the other plan docs, ready to hand to the implementer.

**The MOVE radius is fine.** MOVE is a same-day move: the engine marks a window tile legal only when the hero reaches it today, so a radius of 16 already excludes nothing that needs several days. Farther targets belong to TRAVEL, which offers every area the hero reaches in a day or more on an 18×18 grid per level, with the days to each area as an input, and the hero walks the path as far as today's movement goes. Then MOVE finishes the job once the target is in range. The whole map stays visible at block resolution, so the network sees the far mine or town it is heading for. TRAVEL is not an untrained corner: it is 11% of the live policy's decisions and the teacher labels it. The one gap is a fast hero on a road reaching a tile more than 16 tiles away in one day; that costs two MOVE decisions in the same day instead of one, since the model decides again after each move. On a 144 map a trip may take five TRAVEL days where small maps need one or two; the TRAVEL prior's distance discount covers the part the policy has not practised.

**What the plan builds.** The whole-map grid stays 36×36 cells per level, and a cell becomes a block of `side × side` tiles, where the side is the map's size divided by 36, rounded up. On every map up to 36 the side is 1 and the model runs bit for bit as today. The per-block counts and TRAVEL's areas already work this way in the engine; only the eight tile arrays do not. Everything tile-exact stays tile-exact at any size: the hero windows, MOVE, and every position on the wire.

- **Engine.** The tile loop keeps today's code verbatim at side 1 and summarises a block otherwise, with a fixed, labelled rule for flags, terrain, road, the block's chosen object and its strongest monster.
- **Model.** One integer division where tile positions become grid indices, distances measured in tiles by multiplying block distance by the side, the reach scatter averaged over the window tiles that land in a block, and the side as two zero-initialised embeddings so current checkpoints load unchanged.
- **Knobs.** An eval size that writes to its own CSV, a switch that makes every k-th training game a big map for the one-off experiment, and a per-game wall limit that scales with the map's area while the day caps stay as they are.
- **Acceptance.** Bit-identical outputs at 36 against a golden file and a recorded live minibatch, a synthetic 144 forward with the same output shapes, one headless 144 game against Nullkiller2 whose records decode and run, and the graph-capture check before any deploy.

Small-map training cost is untouched by construction: the wire layout, records, server, batching and CUDA graphs do not change, and the new operations are a division, a multiply and one extra scatter. I measured why the alternative fails your constraint: about 37% of the forward scales with tile count, so a tile-exact 144 grid would cost roughly 6× per decision and need per-size contracts and graphs, and simply raising the tile constant would make every small-map batch XL-shaped. The plan records this and names the fallback if an XL eval shows the block view too coarse: a 72-cell grid class, not a tile-exact one.
