[2026-11-09 17:59] AI: I found one real bug and one design gap that both cost a lot, plus three small issues. Everything was measured on eight finished joint7 games from the PC, replayed with the live checkpoint. I changed nothing in the repo or on the PC.

**1. The teacher's labels loop on visits to our own heroes and towns.** At every decision the advice lets Nullkiller2 plan its turn from scratch and takes its first request (`agents/AlphaMapAI/Advice.cpp`). When its plan starts with one hero visiting another, that visit stays the first request after it has happened. The exchange is carried out our way, so its plan never sees the visit as done. The policy has learned this, since the teacher is about 60% of the gradient.

| Share of MOVEs | Teacher's advice in self-play | Our play | Nullkiller2's own games |
|---|---|---|---|
| Onto our own hero | 55% | 55% | 1.7% |
| Onto our own hero or town | 71% | 74% | 2.5% |

- Meeting our own heroes takes 26% of all movement points, and entering our own towns another 19%.
- 70% of meetings repeat the same pair's meeting from the same day, and about half of those return both armies to an earlier state.
- Right after an exchange the teacher asks the same pair to meet again 54% of the time.
- Exchange decisions are 30% of all training decisions, and no failure metric counts any of this.
- The run's logs show the same exchange share in every update since v1322.

Fix directions, your call:
- Stop teaching an advised move onto a hero that pair already exchanged with that day.
- Make the exchange's label agree with the plan that asked for the meeting.
- Add a learnable prior against a repeat meeting, never a mask.
- Add a metric for repeat meetings in training and in eval.

**2. The credit is one number per player per day.** 96.5% of the advantage's variance is shared by all decisions of a player's day. The live schedule credit in `campaign_model/train.py` is the 7-day outcome minus a baseline, with no step term. The older horizon credit had one.
- On these games the end head explains 82% of the outcome and the 7-day growth head 54%.
- The end head's step is the only per-decision term, and it enters at roughly 13% weight.
- The end head does rate a meeting move below other moves, but the final advantage cannot tell them apart.

I recommend adding a step term for growth and share, mixed with the outcome by trust.

**3. Smaller issues.**
- **Baseline trust:** it is measured on the public heads, while the baseline is the privileged one, which fits twice as well. Full trust would cut the share term's variance by 12%.
- **Teacher weight:** it has been frozen since v1420, so it no longer follows the eval score. This starts to matter once the score passes 0.6.
- **Decision price:** the schedule credit carries none.

**Checked and clean:**
- The model's empire value matches the ledger.

[2026-11-09 18:50] AI: **I found the real cause of the meetings, and it is not what my four "directions" assumed.** Your objections were right: those treated a symptom. Most meeting labels come from a bug inside Nullkiller2 itself. Nothing below is built or run yet; the cause is measured, the effect of the fix is a prediction with a test attached.

## Why the teacher keeps asking for meetings

Nullkiller2 has a task "deliver an army to hero R". It should skip a carrier whose army already includes R's own army. That check fails when R stands still, so the planner counts R's own army as R's reinforcement. The task scores 10,000 to 30,000 against 1,000 to 3,000 for normal tasks, and no exchange can ever satisfy it. I call it the phantom delivery.

Real Nullkiller2 has it too. In one of its own games it sent a scout onto its main hero in all 10 passes of a turn, three turns in a row.

| Measurement | Value |
|---|---|
| Advised meetings that are a delivery task, not a capture chain | 98% |
| Delivery tasks that are the phantom, three games with advice on | 51% to 63% |
| Advised meetings where the visitor holds under a tenth of the other's army | 40% |
| Teacher asks again although 90% or more of the army is with the hero it named | 51% |
| Our exchange rule names the visitor as receiver, against the plan | 39% |
| First exchange choice after an advised meeting is the plan's delivery | 35% |

The last two rows are our own bugs on top:
- **Wrong receiver.** `adviseExchange` picks the higher level, else the stronger army. Nullkiller2's plan gives the army to the hero that was visited.
- **No teacher pressure in the exchange.** The exchange span is ARMY and END only. TAKE_BEST into the wrong hero and TAKE_BEST_FAST are never pushed down, so real deliveries stay open and get asked again.

## The fix

**M1. Remove the phantom.** Nullkiller2 fork, advisor only.
- `Nullkiller.h`: add `bool adviceFixes = false;` beside `keepPlan`, labelled as a fork patch.
- `AINodeStorage`: add public `uint64_t heroMask(const CGHeroInstance * hero) const`. It loops over `actors` and returns `chainMask` of the first actor whose `hero` matches, else 0.
- `GatherArmyBehavior::deliverArmyToHero`, right after the `containsHero` check: `if(aiNk->adviceFixes && (path.chainMask & aiNk->pathfinder->getStorage()->heroMask(receiverHero))) continue;`
- `AlphaMapAI::initAdvice`: set `adviceFixes = true` beside `keepPlan`. The evaluation opponent keeps it off, so eval baselines do not move.

**M2. The exchange's receiver follows the plan.** `AlphaMapAI`.
- In `makeTurn`, at each turn decision, clear `advisedVisit`. If the advice is a MOVE onto a hero of ours and our choice is that same entry, store the mover and the hero met.
- In `adviseExchange`, keep the first line, which picks the hero met. Replace the level and strength override:
  1. If `advisedVisit` is this pair, the destination is the hero met. That is Nullkiller2's own rule in `AIGateway::heroExchangeStarted`.
  2. Otherwise the destination is the hero Nullkiller2 ranks higher: MAIN over SCOUT by `heroManager->getHeroRoleOrDefaultInefficient`, then higher `heroManager->evaluateHero`, then level, then army strength, then the hero met.

**M3. MULTI inside the exchange span.** `train.py`.
- `_teacher_span` gets an `exchange_multi` argument. When true, the exchange row is ARMY, END, MULTI and the label.
- Build both tables. `micro_loss` picks one by a new `config.exchange_span_multi`, default False, so off is bit-identical.
- This is your "NK2-like exchange as one action": TAKE_BEST into the plan's receiver is already accepted by the teacher. Now the other MULTIs are weighed against it. It is a soft loss with no mask, so the credit can still overrule it.
- Run `runtime/check_graphs.py` before deploying.

**M4. The teacher asks for a meeting once per army state.**
- `Nullkiller`: a map from an ordered hero pair to both heroes' armies, each a sorted list of creature id and count.
  - `settleExchange(a, b)` stores the current armies.
  - `exchangeSettled(a, b)` is true while both armies still equal the stored ones, and erases the entry otherwise.
- `AlphaMapAI::exchange`: after its decision loop ends, whatever was chosen, call `settleExchange(first, second)` on the advisor.
- Two checks, both only under `adviceFixes`:
  - `deliverArmyToHero` skips the path when `exchangeSettled(path.targetHero, receiverHero)`.
  - `HeroExchangeMap::tryExchangeNoLock` returns the empty result when both actors are heroes and the pair is settled.
- Nullkiller2 then gives its next best task as the label, so no decision goes unlabelled. Our own actions are untouched.

**M5. Metric.** `failures.py`, in training and eval: meetings, repeat meetings, movement spent on meetings and on entering own towns. Today 54.7% of MOVEs are meetings and they take 25.7% of movement. Real Nullkiller2: 1.7%.

**Tomorrow:** the phantom is gone at the source. A delivery done as taught fails Nullkiller2's own test afterwards. If the model declines, M4 keeps the teacher quiet on that pair until one of the two heroes gains or loses troops, today or tomorrow.

## Town visits: the one real tradeoff, your call

Nullkiller2 takes a town's garrison automatically when its hero visits, and its plans count on that. For us the visit moves nothing, because GATHER has been untaught since the 2026-11-05 collapse. So the teacher teaches the walk without the pickup: 18.7% of all movement.

I recommend teaching GATHER only at the decision right after a hero entered a town on the teacher's advice, as a later deploy behind its own switch. The risk is emptied towns again. The difference from 11-05 is that GATHER was then accepted wherever it was legal.

## The credit

Each decision's credit is the 7-day result minus what the critic expected just before it. A player makes about 25 decisions a day. All 25 share the same 7-day result, and the critic's expectation barely moves within a day. So 96.5% of the credit's variation is between days. On a day with 16 pointless meetings and one good capture, all 17 are pushed the same way.

One correction to my report: the decision's own effect is not missing. It is inside the 7-day result at the same weight as every later decision, so it is buried.

The fix splits the credit in two:
- **Own step:** the critic's forecast at the player's next turn decision that day, minus its forecast here. A wasted move lowers it at once.
- **Rest of the week:** everything after, shared by the whole day.

Today both count fully. The fix keeps the own step and scales the rest by `s = 1 - 0.75 × trust`, the rule the battle credit and the old horizon credit already use.

In `ppo_update`'s schedule block, behind `config.step_credit`, default False:

```python
F = log_phi + (sigmoid(growth_now) * 2 * GROWTH_CAP - GROWTH_CAP)
V = sigmoid(value_now) * 2 * SHARE_CHANGE_CAP - SHARE_CHANGE_CAP
nxt = end["step"]                          # the player's next turn decision, -1 none
same = (nxt >= 0) & (day[nxt] == day)
dF, dV = F[nxt] - F, V[nxt] - V            # used only where same
grow2 = where(same & isfinite(grow), (1 - s_g) * dF + s_g * grow, where(same, dF, grow))
change2 = where(same & isfinite(change), (1 - s_v) * dV + s_v * change, where(same, dV, change))
advantage = w * change2 + (1 - w) * grow2
```

- `s_g` uses `grade_trust()["G7"]`, which is 1.0 now, so 0.25.
- `s_v` uses the privileged critic's own fit when `privileged_credit` is on: a slow average of `1 - value_unexplained_privileged`, over `trust_full_ev`, clipped to `trust_floor` and 1. That is about 0.44 now.
- Pass both through the direct `ppo_update` call and through `self.worker.update`.
- Log the mean step by action type every update.

Replay on 10,879 real decisions:

| | Today | s 0.25 growth, 0.52 share | Both 0.25 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Advantage noise, std | 0.081 | 0.038 | 0.030 |
| Variation shared within a player-day | 98.1% | 85.1% | 65.3% |
| Decisions that get this credit | 82.4% | 98.6% | 98.6% |

The step alone says BUILD +0.0070, exchange MULTI −0.0028, RECRUIT −0.0021, UPGRADE −0.0070. The first two are what we want. RECRUIT and UPGRADE are negative because Φ prices them at a loss, so watch their counts per game after the deploy. If they drop, the fix belongs in Φ's prices.

## Smaller issues

- **Privileged baseline trust:** set `share_trust` to the same number as `s_v`'s trust, inside the step-credit change. It is worth 12% of the share term's variance.
- **Frozen teacher weight:** leave it. `teacher_share_for` returns 0.6 for any score up to 0.6 and the eval is 0.34 to 0.54, so unfreezing changes nothing today.
- **Decision price:** dropped. The step credit prices a wasted action by itself.
- **Correction:** "the end head explains 82%" was inflated by the player count. Over that prior it is 35%.

## Order, one deploy each

1. M5.
2. M1, M2 and M4 together. First play 8 local games with advice on, old build and new build, capped, and compare with the two scripts below. My estimate: meetings fall from 55% of advised MOVEs to under 10%. Then run `type_drift.py`: about 30% of turn labels change at once, the size that hurt on 11-05.

## 1. Cost per action

A useless action moves the critic by about 0, as you say. That is the correct credit for it, but 0 gives no reason to stop, so a price is needed.

The step is less noisy than what we use today:

| Credit | Std |
|---|---|
| The week's outcome, today | 0.073 |
| One decision's own step | 0.013 |

Wasted moves do show in it. After a move onto our own hero V_end falls 0.27e-3, and after other moves it rises 0.72e-3.

Taking the cost out of the D+2/5/7 rewards fails for three reasons:
1. Every decision of that day gets the same deduction, the useful ones too.
2. The value heads would have to learn how many actions a day will have.
3. After the baseline, what remains is mostly a bonus for ending the day early.

What I built is `step_price = 2e-4`, subtracted from the credit of the decision that took the action. END and questions are free. An average MOVE's own step is 6.5e-4 and a BUILD's is 7e-3, so a useless action turns slightly negative and a normal move still pays.

Improvements I could predict, done now:
- **Share step scaling:** it used the raw forecast while its baseline used a scaled one. Both now use the same.
- **Share step trust:** it was the baseline's regression slope, which is not a measure of fit. It now has its own, `forecast_trust`.
- **TensorBoard:** each action type's mean step is logged under `campaign_step/*`, so the critic's habits are visible. After an UPGRADE, G7 falls 0.0070 while the empire value loses 0.0002.
- **Per-type correction:** built, measured, left off. It doubled every type's bias, RECRUIT from −0.22σ to −0.44σ.

Replay on 8 real joint7 games, 10,879 decisions:

**What it is.** For each decision, the credit is how much the critic's forecast of our empire value 7 days ahead changed between this decision and our next one that day, minus the tiny price. The forecast is the empire value now plus the G7 head's predicted growth. Gold counts in the empire value at face value, so picking it up raises the forecast at once.

I measured it on the 4,589 MOVEs of the 8 real joint7 games:

| What the move did | Moves | Mean step | Positive |
|---|---|---|---|
| Collected gold, 250 or more | 96 | +0.0209 | 97% |
| Collected gold, 1000 or more | 41 | +0.0261 | 98% |
| No gold, empire value up 0.5% or more | 831 | +0.0029 | 50% |
| No gold, empire value unchanged | 2,179 | −0.0007 | 45% |
| Every MOVE | 4,589 | +0.00065 | 48% |

The price is 0.0002 on top of that. The unit is the log of empire value, so +0.021 means the 7-day forecast rose about 2.1%.

Three things to read from the table:
- **Gold pickups:** +0.021 is about twice the step's own noise of 0.011. The critic also raises its growth forecast after a pickup, so the step is larger than the gold alone.
- **Moves that change nothing:** these are 47% of all moves. They are already slightly negative before the price, because movement was spent for nothing. With the price they are −0.0009.
- **Gains the critic expected:** the third row gained value but scored only +0.003. The credit rewards doing better than the critic expected, not the raw gain.

The week's real outcome is still in the credit, at a smaller weight, so it corrects the critic when the critic is wrong.

`step_credit` is still off and not deployed.

## Cost per action in the 7-day reward

Built as `schedule_action_price`, off by default, on my branch at commit `2466290`. It is not in tonight's deploy, so tonight shows the meeting fixes alone. It goes on as its own deploy, last in the order, at your 2e-6.

It charges each decision for the actions the player makes from that decision on through its 7-day window. Actions before the decision are not counted, because the decision could not have caused them. Measured on the 8 games, a decision has 107 actions ahead of it in its week.

| Price per action | Charge vs outcome spread |
|---|---|
| 2e-6 | 0.30% |
| 7e-6 | about 1% |
| 2e-5, your cap | 3.0% |

With fewer steps the charge gets smaller, not larger, since it is the count times the price. At 2e-6, one action is 0.003% of the spread, so do not expect to see any effect within a night.

On average yes, and I checked it against what actually happened. I compared the real value a week later with the forecast the critic made right after the purchase.

| Purchase | Value lost at once | Real result vs forecast |
|---|---|---|
| BUILD paid by trades, 68 cases | −8.7% | −0.9% ± 0.8% |
| Other BUILDs, 239 cases | none | −0.8% ± 0.5% |
| RECRUIT paid by trades, 45 cases | −4.8% | −2.6% ± 0.7% |

Had the critic missed the 8.7%, the real result would sit 8.7% under its forecast. It sits 0.9% under, the same as for any other build. For recruits it is too optimistic by 2.6%. Overall it explains 54% of the real 7-day growth, so it is right on average and not precise per case.

**What happened**

A battle with both sides played by our model reached a state where nothing could be damaged and neither side could retreat. Our stalemate rule only ends such a battle when one side can retreat, so it kept going: 1,723 decisions in 62 silent seconds, and the client grew to 3.8 GB holding the battle record. The watchdog kills a game after 60 seconds without output, so the game and its record were lost.

The run's log holds 298 such watchdog kills in 9.5 days, about 1.3 an hour, from several causes. Tonight's rate is the usual one. Five of the campaign-game kills were on this same map, Irrational Hostility. I have not confirmed that all five had this exact cause.

**The fix**

When 50 rounds pass with no damage and neither side can retreat, the battle ends and the side whose living army is worth more wins. That completes the existing rule, where only the side that is behind gives up.

[2026-11-10 06:41] AI: The stalled eval game b1 flagged was a real bug in Nullkiller2's end-of-turn code. It is fixed and deployed, and the run has been training normally since 06:35.

**The bug**
- The stalled game was in the eval before the switch (v2652, 04:25), not in the 0.511 eval; that one had no stall.
- Nullkiller2's thread that ends a turn re-sends the request while a "my turn" flag is up. When the other player's turn takes about 70 ms (our player with nothing to do on a 2-player map), Nullkiller2's next turn has already raised that flag.
- The old thread then ends the new turn as it begins, the server refuses the new turn's requests, two turn threads run at once, and the client deadlocks.
- 13 eval games were killed this way in 151 evals. All five kept samples show the same signature. Each was played again, so scores were not lost, only eval time.
- It only affects evals, since Nullkiller2 does not play training games.

**The fix** (engine commit `d7868e680`, main `897db08`, local only)
- One file: the end-of-turn loop re-sends only while it is still the same turn.
- Reproduced first by forcing the race locally: the old code got a request refused and hung at day 9, and the fixed code played the same game to its end.

**Deploy at 06:35**
- It also carried the model server fix from earlier (a request for a model that is not loaded no longer blocks the other requests).
- PC checks passed: server tests, a Nullkiller2-only game on the map of the incident (331 turns, none refused), two games of our model against Nullkiller2, and an advised game pair, all without errors.
- The run resumed at version 2695 with no error lines, and the Mac worker is back with 9 slots.

## What is broken

One update's gradient rests on very few battles. Measured on today's saved update (168 battles, 98 games):

Weight each decision by 1 / (1 + (n − 1) / 30), where n is the number of decisions in its battle, so a battle counts as at most about 30 decisions. On today's battles the gradient then rests on 30 games for the policy (from 14) and 28 for the value (from 4), with no extra compute.

- **It raises the signal from 0.5% to a few percent at best**, if every game carries equal signal. That is an improvement, not a guarantee of learning.
- **The slow steady drift is unexplained.** b1 pointed out that the weights have drifted in a steady direction for over 1,000 updates without moving the eval. So that direction either does not improve play or changes with the battle mix. Testing which needs the PC.
- **Today's credit settings are unmeasured.** The 0.5% is for Oct 31 to Nov 5; measuring the period since needs the PC's newer checkpoints.

- The other level is never a MOVE target. To go down, the hero moves onto the gate's tile, and the next decision's window is centered where it comes out. The other way is TRAVEL: 2 levels × 18 × 18 = 648 areas, each with the pathfinder's days to reach it. TRAVEL is scored the same way: a learned match plus the area's value discounted by those days.
- 8,712 (8 × 33 × 33) is the table's size. The legal entries are only the tiles each hero can reach today.

There are three weak spots:
- The price can't see through a gate. Φ prices gates, monoliths and whirlpools at nothing, since they're "worth what they lead to" (docs/empire_value.md:147). So MOVE's price for stepping onto one is only the land it reveals around it. Using a gate has to come from the learned match, or from TRAVEL.
- The tile can't see the other level either. The U-Net runs on each level separately (campaign_model/model_v2.py:604), and no input says where a gate or monolith leads. Information from the other level reaches a pair only through the hero token, which reads both levels, and through the pathfinder's numbers. So the slide's "both read from the whole game" overstates it for the tile: the tile has only seen its own level, with heroes and towns stamped on it.
- Fast heroes outrun the window. A hero on roads can get more than 16 tiles in a day; those tiles are reachable only through TRAVEL.

2. No architecture for the learned part. That's fine for this slide, which is about the scoring rule and is already full. It's not fine for the deck. The slide's main claim, that the match knows who should go because it has seen the whole game, rests on a network the audience never sees, and as shown above the claim is partly overstated. That network also has ideas worth showing:
- heroes and towns stamped onto the map before the U-Net (AlphaStar's scatter connections);
- tokens reading the map through attention, weighted by distance and by each hero's reach;
- a memory carried from one decision to the next;
- foresight: before deciding, the model predicts the engine's answer to each candidate move. Does the monster attack, flee or join? What's P(win), and what share of the hero's army and value would it cost? These predictions are trained on the engine's real answers. A second transformer pass and MOVE's scorer both build on them.

I'd add one slide on the network right before this one, laid out like AlphaStar's architecture slide, with foresight as its trick.

❯ "The other level is never a MOVE target." This seems wrong. Would it not be better to take the closest 8,712 points as alternatives regardless of if they need a gate or not? is it doable in a reasonable amount of time? Also maybe for gate/enterence we need to have some different embeddings based on if their endpoint is visible... I'm not sure what is the right solution here.

You're right. "The other level is never a MOVE target" correctly describes the code, since the window is built on the hero's own level (agents/AlphaMapAI/Encoder.cpp:213). But that design is wrong, and not just in a corner case: our maps all have an underground (campaign_model/config.py:29, levels = 2). Today a hero gets past a gate in one of two ways:
- a MOVE onto the gate, which the price values at 0, then a second MOVE;
- a TRAVEL to an area on the other side.

Either way, the mine past the gate is never priced as a MOVE.

Your fix is the right one. "Closest" should mean by the pathfinder's cost (days, then movement used), not tile distance. Give each hero the 1,089 tiles it can reach soonest, on either level, through any gate, monolith or boat the pathfinder uses. (8,712 is the total over 8 heroes, so the table keeps its size.) This also fixes two other weaknesses:
- road tiles more than 16 away become MOVE targets;
- no slots are wasted on rocks and water inside the square.

Gate embeddings and visible endpoints. The split you suggest is real, and VCMI already makes it. Its pathfinder routes through a teleport only once the player has revealed the exit's tile (getTeleportChannelExits filters exits by visibility; worth confirming in our fork).
- Exit revealed: needs nothing new. The tiles past it show up as ordinary candidates, priced by what they hold.
- Exit not revealed: this is the only case that needs an input, typically a hero's first trip through a gate. Add one flag on the entrance, taken from VCMI's teleport-channel data. Price it as a full sight of new land, since everything around an unseen exit is unexplored.

Is it doable? Yes, in about two days of work, mostly in Python.
- C++ (small): the hero's paths info already covers both levels (Encoder.cpp:645-700). Collect the reachable tiles, sort them by cost, keep 1,089, and write each slot's position as a new input. A MOVE then goes to its slot's position. Picking the right exit along the path is already handled (AlphaMapAI.cpp:1146).
- Python (the real work): five places assume a square around the hero:
  - guard zones (features.py:523, 529);
  - land revealed (features.py:546);
  - what a guard blocks (features.py:927);
  - positions, the hero's own tile and the dx/dy features (model.py:1065-1069, 1220, 1277);
  - the metrics (failures.py:54).

  The square-grid calculations get replaced by three raw facts C++ passes for each slot: its guard, whether the path crosses a guard, and how many hidden tiles a visit would reveal. They're raw engine facts like the pathfinder's numbers, so the behaviour still lives in Python.
- Compatibility: with 1,089 slots kept, the tensor shapes, checkpoints and CUDA graphs don't change. The new inputs (level change, path through a teleport, unseen exit) start at 0. Old game records get slot positions from their square when loaded.

Two things to watch:
- Dimension Door: tile-target spells share the window, but their targets aren't path-based, so they need a few geometric slots of their own.
- Label shift: Nullkiller 2's advised targets past a gate will become MOVE labels instead of TRAVEL or gate-step labels. That's a label change, so measure the type drift after the first update.

## What I decided

I did not build the "closest 1,089 tiles by path cost" list. The window features read a tile's neighbours and the unreachable land behind a guard (guard zones, land a step reveals, what a guard blocks). A reach-ordered list would have moved that into C++ and lost "what a guard blocks".

Instead each hero gets **one more square window**, placed in a window slot no hero is using (we run about 2.8 heroes in 8 slots). It is a square of whichever level holds the most tiles the hero reaches today outside its own window. Its tiles are MOVE targets with the same features and price as the hero's own window. Checkpoint shapes are unchanged and older records read as before.

For your second point (a gate whose exit is visible or not): VCMI's pathfinder only goes through a teleporter to an exit we have seen.
- **Exit seen:** the tiles past it show up in the extra window, nothing else needed.
- **Exit not seen:** the entrance gets a new flag. MOVE prices it as a full sight of new land, TRAVEL treats its area as unrevealed, and the tile encoder has a vector for it that starts at 0. Whirlpools are not priced, since they cost troops.

## What I measured

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Hero-turns with tiles in reach today outside the own window (Nullkiller2 game, 40 days) | 43%, median 31 tiles against 77 inside |
| Tiles a second / third extra window would add | median 8 / 3, hence the cap of one |
| New code against the deployed code, same weights and inputs, no extra window | 42 outputs and features, difference 0 |
| Moves made through an extra window (our AI, one game) | 16, all had an effect; all 14 I could follow ended on the target's level |
| Nullkiller2 labels that land in an extra window | 18 of 865 advised MOVE labels, 32 of 1,192 accepted entries |
| Game client CPU per decision, with / without | 4.4–4.7 ms / 4.5–4.6 ms |
| Model forward on the Mac's CPU | 27.2 ms at 3 windows, +1.6 ms per extra window |
| Tests | campaign 304 pass, battle 191 pass |

The PC's GPU inference already computes all 8 slots, so it sees no change. Training's window budget of 4 per decision will overflow with about one extra window per decision; it should go to 5 when the feature is turned on.

## Not done

- **Second teleport in one day:** tiles neither window shows still take two decisions.
- **Tile features across levels:** the map network still reads each level separately, so a tile's own vector does not know what is past a gate. The hero–tile pair is informed through the extra window. Linking the two ends inside the network is not built.

- The main checkout is now on branch `move-windows`, and its `build/` holds the new AI libraries. The ref `main` is unchanged and equals the PC.

[2026-11-10 23:59] AI: No, today it really is gold, and your objection is fair.

**What the code does**

- The stake is gold: the hero's army plus the hero's worth plus the cost of replacing them.
- It is multiplied by the chance of losing the hero tonight and added to the tile's other values in gold (the pickup, the fight danger).
- That sum goes through a log squash before it becomes a logit, so it is never raw gold in a layer. The network's inputs are untouched; this is only in the logit priors.
- It is still unbounded, only slowly:

| Gold at stake | Logit |
|---|---|
| 550 | 2.2 |
| 4,000 | 3.3 |
| 10,000 | 4.0 |
| 40,000 | 5.3 |
| 200,000 | 6.9 |
| 1,000,000 | 8.5 |

So it grows with map size and game day, which is exactly what you ruled out for features, and above your "more than 4 is crazy" line for any army over 10k.

**Why not just the %**

The only reason it is gold is that it sits in one sum with the pickup on the same tile, and pickups are priced in gold (Nullkiller2's values). If only the night term were a share, a share-priced loss and a gold-priced chest on one tile could not be compared. That is a reason to convert the whole sum, not a reason to keep gold.

A share of our empire is the better unit: bounded by 100%, the same on any map and day, and the unit the reward is already in. I asked b1 to build it behind a switch (everything inside that squash as a share of our empire's value, scaled so the first days read as today). I will paired-test it on the 48 eval maps before anything goes to the PC, because the network has trained 2,900 updates against the gold prior and a flatter late-game prior could hurt at first.

**The learned preference beating the prior**

Agreed, and nothing I deployed removes that. The night term is a prior; the network's own logits still sit on top and can override it. My complaint was about why it was learned: nothing in self-play punished it. That is why the next item matters.

**One thing that needs your eye: `night_gain` is frozen**

So in the collapse it went exactly as you describe: behaviour changed, V got worse, and its loss took up to a third or more of the shared layers' gradient while the policy sat on top of them. Last night V barely moved, so it cannot be what moved the policy then.

**The fix: shield the policy from V only while V is off, automatically.**

One reading drives it: how far the fresh value loss stands above its calm level (the guard already computes this every update).

1. **Valve on V's path into the shared layers.** When the value loss is at its calm level, nothing changes. As it rises, the gradient the value loss sends into the shared layers is scaled down in proportion (to a floor of about 10%). V's own layer and heads keep their full gradient and their faster rate, so V re-fits at full speed while the policy's features are not dragged.
2. **Valve on the policy's reward term.** Its weight is scaled down by the same ratio (floor about 20%) while V is off, so the policy does not learn from advantages built on a stale V. The teacher term stays as the anchor.
3. The hard stop at 3 times stays as the last resort.

This gives "let V converge first" after every behaviour change without a second network, with no extra compute and no checkpoint change. I did not route the second valve through the credit's trust in V: that was tried on 2026-11-06 and made the credit noisier.

It cannot be paired-tested (it changes training, not play), so its checks are unit tests, the GPU update check, and the readings through GATHER's ramp. I asked b1 to attack the design before building it.

[2026-11-11 07:50] AI: It is a good idea, a well-known family, and probably the right long-term structure. I would change two things in it, and there is a cheap test that tells us whether it pays; b1 is setting that up now.

**Was it tried before**

- Separate policy and value networks with value knowledge passed back to the policy network is [Phasic Policy Gradient](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.04416) (OpenAI, 2020). The policy network carries an auxiliary value head and is periodically distilled from value targets, with a KL term that holds the policy fixed while its features change. It was built for exactly your complaint: sharing gives useful features, sharing also lets the objectives interfere.
- AlphaStar used a fully separate value network with privileged information and no feature link to the policy.
- I found no paper doing your exact link, a penalty between the two last hidden states. A 2025 study, [Studying the Interplay Between Actor and Critic Representations](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/57da66da25d0ce77e0129b246f358851-Paper-Conference.pdf), is relevant to it: when separated, the actor's features specialise in action-relevant information and the critic's in value and dynamics.

**What I would change**

1. **The hidden-state penalty reopens the channel you want closed.** When V re-fits after a behaviour change, its hidden state moves, and the penalty drags P's hidden state after it, which moves the policy. It is a slower version of the drag we have today. Phasic Policy Gradient avoids this by holding the policy's outputs fixed (a KL on the action distribution) while the features are transferred.
2. **Match what V predicts, not V's whole hidden state.** KL is not defined between hidden vectors (it would be an L2 or cosine penalty), and forcing the vectors equal fights the specialisation above. An auxiliary value head on P, trained to reproduce V's outputs, gives P the value-relevant features without the rest.

On auxiliary losses: the prediction ones (survival, battle outcomes) belong with V, and reach P through the distillation. The teacher's loss is a policy loss and stays with P.

**Cost**

- Using V's hidden state or outputs from before its update costs nothing extra: they are computed anyway for V's own loss. Using them after the update costs one more V forward per batch, roughly 15-20% of an update, and buys nothing at these learning rates.
- The real cost is the second trunk: about twice the learner's compute and GPU memory per update. The learner is already the bottleneck (an update takes about 170 s of a 175-190 s cycle), so updates per hour would roughly halve unless V trains on fewer steps.
- Games are unchanged, since only P plays.
- No restart is needed: both networks can start as copies of the live checkpoint.

**Is it better than the valves**

They solve different amounts of the problem.

| | Valves (live now) | Two networks with distillation |
|---|---|---|
| Stops a noisy V dragging the policy | only while the value loss is above its recent level | always, by construction |
| Lets V learn its own features | no | yes |
| Cost | none | about 2 times learner compute, a migration, days to validate |
| Hand-set constants | three (floor, rate limit, averaging window) | distillation weight and schedule |

You are right that the valves are a patch. I deployed them because they cost nothing and protect the GATHER ramp today, not because they are the final structure.

The argument for your design that I find strongest is not interference. It is that today the shared layers are shaped 60% by the teacher, about 20% by the policy and 5% by the value, and the value's fit is poor (explained variance 0.17-0.20). A V with its own trunk might fit much better, and a better V means better advantages for a policy whose gradient is mostly noise.

**How to know without an expensive check**

That last point is measurable offline today. b1 is setting up this test on the Mac, on recorded training games, split by game into train and held-out, all three arms from the same checkpoint with equal steps:

- **A:** trained as the run is, every loss on the shared network.
- **B:** a copy trained on the value losses only, whole trunk free. This is your V.
- **C:** trunk frozen, value layers only. This is what the valve leaves at its floor.

A shuffled-label control guards against B simply memorising the training games.

- If B's held-out value fit is clearly better than A's, the split pays and I build it in the form above.
- If it is not, the value targets are the limit, and the split would only buy what the valves already give.

The test also records how far B's hidden state moves per step, which is exactly what your penalty would transmit to P. I'll report size and timing once b1 confirms the data.

Sources:
- [Phasic Policy Gradient](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.04416)
- [Studying the Interplay Between Actor and Critic Representations (ICLR 2025)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/57da66da25d0ce77e0129b246f358851-Paper-Conference.pdf)
- [No Representation, No Trust: Connecting Representation, Collapse, and Trust Issues in PPO](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.00662)

**The fade is broken**

The rule you set was "the teacher's share follows how good we are". The weight still follows the eval score, but since the loss shares were frozen (v1420) the teacher's share of the shared layers' gradient is pinned at 60% whatever the weight says. So at a score of 0.5 it still takes 60% of every update, against about 20% for the policy's reward. That is the setup your worry describes: imitation got us off the ground and now holds most of the gradient.

**Three end states**

1. **Keep the loss, fix its labels** (the hero-order problem).
2. **Fade the loss out** and let reward plus the priors drive.
3. **Move Nullkiller2 from a loss to an input**, as you suggest: its priority for each task it considers, mapped to our actions, enters as a logit prior with a learned, decayed correction. That is your own rule for "a value the existing AI already assigns", it is attributable per action, and the loss fades out. The policy then starts from Nullkiller2's choice and learns only where reward disagrees, with nothing pulling it back. This is known as residual policy learning; fading a distillation loss as the student improves is the "kickstarting" recipe.

I lean toward 3 if it is feasible, with 2 as the fallback. I do not want to pick before one number.

b1's play-the-labels test is about to start: our policy against an arm that plays Nullkiller2's matched advice at every decision. Its score is exactly the level a policy would start from if Nullkiller2's choice were its prior.

[2026-11-11 09:15] AI: **Yes, remove the teacher's loss, and keep its knowledge by computing it ourselves, not by feeding its scores in.** Its scores only mean something within one decision, its plan flips on 35% of quiet decisions, and we would need Nullkiller2 running at every decision forever. What transfers is what it looks at and how it combines it.

## Why imitating it is hard now

Nullkiller2 scores (hero, object, path) with about 15 quantities, then hands out one task per hero, best score first. Our logits are (hero, tile reachable today) and (hero, area), each seen from that hero alone. Where both sides look at the same thing, imitation was learned almost for free. Where it decides in a space we do not represent, 3,000 updates at 60% of the shared gradient did not learn it. This is b1's measurement on 17,400 advised decisions:

| Decision kind | Share of decisions | Agreement | Share of the teacher's loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exchange (both armies on the table) | 21.6% | 0.82 | 1.4% |
| Only one hero can act | 25.3% | 0.28 | 24.7% |
| Label moves the hero we moved | 15.7% | 0.46 | 25.1% |
| Label moves another hero | 16.1% | 0.28 | 31.4% |

The second row matters most. With no order question at all, we pick its target 28% of the time. Your hero-order worry is real but the smaller part; target choice is the main miss.

## What it knows that we do not

This is my reading of its evaluator and planner against our features, not yet measured.

| Nullkiller2 has | We have | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Closest-hero ratio: every task's score is multiplied by the nearest hero's cost over this hero's cost | Nothing compares our heroes on a target | Compute it from the days each hero needs, already an input for areas; one new raw input for today's tiles |
| One task per hero, one hero per target, chosen jointly | Each decision scores its own hero; the plan head is a label, never an input | Feed each hero's current target back as an input (the model's own previous output), plus "another hero is headed there" on every target |
| For targets a day or more away: the object's own reward, army lost in every fight on the path, enemy danger on arrival | TRAVEL's known part prices an area by object-class counts and days; MOVE has the rest, but only for today's tiles | Price areas from the per-tile values MOVE uses, plus the guards on the path |
| Enemy reach in turns, by real paths, per tile and town | Straight-line distance, 15 tiles, same level only | C++ passes the days each seen enemy hero needs to our towns and heroes; Python does the rest |
| Tiers: kill today, defend today, kill, gather or explore, escape, defend; a higher tier always wins | One additive value | A few flags with zero-init weights |

Already ours: hero roles, gold pressure, recruit pause, skill scores, building rewards, fight loss and win, exploration, movement discount, the home/defend/ferry pulls.

The per-action score you want is our own prior once it has these terms. The dense plan is the second row: one target vector per hero, attributable to tiles and areas directly.

## The plan

Each step gets a paired test on the Mac before the PC, one per deploy.

0. **Readout test, today, offline.** Freeze the trunk and fit at most 64 new weights on the recorded labels, holding out games. Per decision kind it shows how far a short readout of our top layer gets, with and without the candidate features. Kinds that stay low name what to build first. I asked b1 to run it after its current test.
1. Cross-hero features.
2. TRAVEL priced like MOVE.
3. Each hero's target as an input.
4. Enemy reach by real paths. This also fixes the night term across levels and on large maps.
5. Teacher's weight ramped to zero, with stop rules like GATHER's. GATHER then needs its own prior.

Nothing here runs Nullkiller2 at play time, trains against it, or uses absolute gold. Its evaluation log stays useful offline only, to check that our "army lost on the path" matches its number.

## On surpassing it quickly

- **Where we are:** about half of it, not at parity: 0.50 on the eval's scale, where it scores 1.0 itself.
- **Where gains came from:** the two I can prove were knowledge added as priors: run-away +0.077 ± 0.023 and unseen exits +0.059 ± 0.025. Learning has added nothing I can separate from noise.
- **Why learning is weak:** on held-out games the critic explains 3 to 13% of the share change over 2 to 7 days.
- **So:** steps 1 to 4 are the fast part, a few hours each to test. Step 5 is what lets learning go past it afterwards.

Step 5 is the risky one, because it removes the steadiest gradient the trunk gets. If the policy drifts, the answer is a slower ramp, not the teacher back.

b1's test that plays the matched advice through our actions calibrates all of this. If that arm scores near 1.0, knowledge is the gap and this plan stands. If it scores near ours, the action mapping is the gap and the list changes.

[2026-11-11 10:11] AI: You're right: the first version listed fields. In this version every number sits on a vector the model already builds for a hero and a tile, in a unit the model already uses, and in the combined form a decision needs.

## What exists today

- For every tile in a hero's window the model builds a **pair vector**: hero embedding + tile embedding + how this hero reaches the tile + the fight there. MOVE scores a tile from its pair vector. TRAVEL does the same for (hero, area).
- The tile's expected value on arrival exists, in gold, passed through one fixed squashing into logit units.
- Two weaknesses of exactly the kind you describe:
  - Days in the window are a one-hot (never, today, 1, 2, 3+), i.e. a day embedding.
  - A step toward a far destination is scored from the step's own tile, which is empty.

## Rules

1. A new number is a channel on an existing (hero, tile) or (hero, area) pair, never a free-standing row. It then meets the hero and tile embeddings in the layer that scores that pair.
2. Four units only, each on the scale of the feature it sits beside:
   - value in logit units;
   - fight odds as a log strength ratio and a loss share;
   - time as a discount;
   - preference as a gap to the best alternative.
3. Each number comes alone and already combined the way a decision uses it.
4. A first step carries its destination.

## Each quantity

| Quantity | Representation | Why it is easy to read |
|---|---|---|
| Time to a tile | Arrival time `t` in fractional days (share of today's movement spent, then whole days plus the last day's share). Fed as two discounts: `1/(1+t)` and `1/(1+t/3)` | Any discount between a one-day and a three-day half-life is a weighted sum of the two. No integer, no embedding per day |
| Value on arrival (ours, exists) | Adds value × each discount, in the same logit unit | "Value per time" is given, not learned as a product |
| Relative value (ours, new) | Discounted value minus this hero's best option, and minus the best of any hero; clamped to [−8, 0], scaled to [−1, 0] | 0 means "the best this hero can do". Says which hero should act and on what |
| Nullkiller2's priority | A float from hand formulas; only ratios within one decision mean anything. Fed as `ln(priority / decision's best)` and `ln(priority / this hero's best)`, clamped to [−4, 0], plus a "has a candidate" flag | Its formula is a product (reward × (1 − loss) ÷ time). The log turns that into a sum, which is what our logits are |
| Its army loss on the path | Share 0 to 1, the unit of our own fight-loss feature; also × what the hero carries, as a share of our empire | Sits beside our loss for the fight at the tile; the cost of the trip is comparable with the value |
| Its danger on arrival | Log of our strength over theirs, plus a "hopeless" term: the same three numbers as our fight features | Reuses a form the model already acts on |
| Its time (paths through guards, teleporters, meetings) | The same two discounts, plus a flag "our pathfinder cannot reach it" | Same unit as our own time |
| Kind of task | One-hot of six (visit, attack hero, attack town, defend, meet our hero, explore) | A category, not a number |

Its reward numbers (gold, army, skill, strategic) are not imported. They are in its own mixed units and duplicate our tile values.

## A first step carries its destination

- Each candidate gives a hero, a destination tile and today's stopping tile on the path (or a TRAVEL area).
- The entry for that first step gets the destination's pair vector, through a zero-init projection.
- It also gets the destination's numbers: discounted value, preference gaps, loss, danger, remaining time.
- An entry that is itself the destination carries itself.
- A destination outside the hero's window uses its (hero, area) pair, which exists map-wide.
- When several candidates share a first step, the entry gets the best one plus the summed preference behind that step.

## The plan as a vector

- Each hero's token gets a preference-weighted average of its destinations' tile embeddings (zero-init). Because this is added before the heroes attend to each other, the model can sort out who goes where.
- Each entry also gets "another hero of ours is headed here".

## Default weight

Nullkiller2's preference gap is the one value "the old AI assigns", so by your priors rule it gets a fixed weight β on first-step and arrival entries, with β set by paired test. Everything else enters through zero-init weights.

## Wire

64 candidate rows of about 12 numbers each, under 1% of what a decision sends today. No new per-tile field.

## Gate before anything trains

This is the test of "can the network learn it intuitively". b1 refits the small readout from our prior alone with these channels, on about 200 recorded games.

- It must beat the trained policy's fit of Nullkiller2 (1.51).
- It must put Nullkiller2's label first on at least 70% of TRAVEL and MOVE-onto-object decisions that have a candidate (today 29% and 50%).
- If about 64 weights cannot do that, the representation is wrong and gets fixed first.

[2026-11-11 10:27] AI: Revised plan below. The main change is that value is now counted the same several bounded ways in every layer, and everything else follows your comments.

## One way to count value, used everywhere

Any gold amount `g` that enters a learned layer goes through the same six views. All are smooth, signed, and stay inside −1 to 1.

| View | Formula | Half-way point |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute, fine | `g / (abs(g) + 2,000)` | 2,000 gold |
| Absolute, coarse | `g / (abs(g) + 20,000)` | 20,000 gold |
| Share of our empire, fine | `s / (abs(s) + 0.02)`, `s = g / our empire value` | 2% of the empire |
| Share of our empire, coarse | `s / (abs(s) + 0.2)` | 20% of the empire |
| Days of our own growth | `p / (abs(p) + 1)`, `p = g / our daily gain` | one day's growth |
| Weeks of our own growth | `p / (abs(p) + 7)` | one week's growth |

- **Daily gain:** our empire value's average gain per day over the last 7 days, floored at 0.5% of the empire. I use the week because one day's change swings negative after a lost battle. It needs one new input: the model's own empire-value output from 7 days ago, passed back.
- **Where it applies:**
  - tile values (object, fight return, what a guard blocks, the night's loss);
  - a fight's stake and gain;
  - hero worth and army worth;
  - town value;
  - building rewards and costs, recruit and hire costs, trade losses;
  - our empire value for the critic.
- **Current checkpoint versus a clean start:** on the current checkpoint the views are appended beside today's encodings with zero-init weights. On a clean start today's ad-hoc encodings go, including the unbounded log.

## Time: two features

| Feature | Definition | Fed as |
|---|---|---|
| Own time | Days this hero needs, fractional | `1/(1+t)` and `1/(1+t/3)` |
| Baseline time | The path's movement points / 1,500 (a baseline hero's day) | The same two discounts |

A fast hero then shows a short own time and an ordinary baseline time, so speed is visible and not normalised away. This needs one new per-tile field: movement points left on arrival for tiles reached on later days (today it is sent only for tiles reached today).

## Value with time

- **Value on arrival:** the six views of the tile's value.
- **Value per day of movement:** `g / (t + 0.25)`, once with own time and once with baseline time. Each goes through three views (absolute coarse, share fine, days of growth). The quarter-day floor means a pickup beside the hero counts at most 4 times its value.
- **Relative value:** the gap to this hero's best option and to any hero's best, as `−tanh(gap / 4)`, inside −1 to 0.

## Nullkiller2's numbers

| Quantity | Representation | Bound |
|---|---|---|
| Priority | `−tanh(ln(best / priority) / 3)`, against the decision's best and against this hero's best | −1 to 0, never flat |
| Danger on arrival | `risk = r² / (1 + r²)`, `r = their strength / ours`, plus today's soft-bounded "hopeless" term | 0 to 1, one-sided |
| Army loss on the path | The share itself, and `ln(1 − loss + 0.01)` | 0 to 1, and −4.6 to 0 |
| Its own time | The same discounts as ours | 0 to 1 |
| Kind, settled, other-hero-headed-here | One-hot and 0 to 1 values, as before | |

- **Danger is one-sided.** When we are far stronger the risk flattens at 0. Nothing grows because a fight is easy, so pixies beside a strong hero add nothing; whether to kill them is left to the value of doing so. Today's four strength features are symmetric (bounded at ±2). They would go on a clean start.
- **The log of path loss is finite at certain death and never loses its gradient.** It touches only the entries of that one path, so flooding them is acceptable, as you said.

## Weights that cannot start with the wrong sign

- **Known direction:** the direct weight is a bounded gain with a fixed sign and a small non-zero start, the pattern the priors already use.
  - Path loss and risk can only lower an entry (range 0 to 2, start 0.25).
  - Nullkiller2's preference can only raise it (β, by paired test).
- **Unknown direction:** zero-init free weights. This covers task kind, settled, other-hero-headed-here and the plan vector.
- Every feature also feeds the free nonlinear layer, whose output starts at zero.

## Unchanged from the last version

- New numbers sit on existing (hero, tile) and (hero, area) pairs.
- A first step carries its destination's pair vector.
- The plan vector is built from destination tile embeddings.
- 16 candidates per hero.
- The plan head stays and is fed back.

## Gates before anything trains

1. **Readable:** the small readout from our prior must beat the trained policy's fit (1.51) and put Nullkiller2's label first on at least 70% of TRAVEL and MOVE-onto-object decisions that have a candidate.
2. **No explosion, nothing dead:** over 200 recorded games, every new channel stays inside its stated bound, and its 1st-to-99th percentile range covers at least a tenth of that bound. A view that sits saturated for every tile gets its scale fixed first.

**The plan while you're away:**
- I make fixes one at a time, each with a short check, and give you one report when you're back.

**The advantage-regression idea, explained better:**

- **Today:** the policy learns only by "this game went well, so make everything you did a bit more likely". Every decision in a day gets nearly the same credit (98% shared). A good move and a bad move on the same day are pushed the same way, so over many games the pushes cancel into noise.
- **The fix:** add a small head that predicts, for each legal entry (this tile, this build), how much better or worse the outcome is than the average choice at that decision. It is trained like the critic, by plain regression on what happened after the entry was played.
- **Why regression works where the policy push doesn't:** a regression averages over every game it ever sees, so noise cancels across thousands of games. The policy push must find the signal inside one update of about 14 games. The critic's weights already move consistently (0.50) while the policy's do not (0.20).
- **How the policy uses it:** the predicted advantage is added to the entry's logit with a learnable gain that starts at zero. The policy then shifts toward entries the head has seen do well, as fast as the head fits.
- **Why it fits now:** we play NK2's choice 90% of the time, which gives a well-measured baseline at every decision. The 10% where we leave it are the samples that say whether leaving was better.
- **What could make it fail:** if one decision's effect on the outcome is too small to see even after averaging, the head predicts zero and nothing changes. That is the under-10-minute check on recorded games I will run before building it.

[2026-11-11 15:57] USER: "how much better or worse the outcome is than the average choice at that decision. It is trained like the critic, by plain regression on what happened after the entry was played." where do the action level labels come from?

[2026-11-11 15:57] AI: There are no action-level labels. The label is the same per-decision advantage the policy already uses, and my wording made it sound more specific than it is.

**What the label is:** for each decision we played, the change in our empire share over the credit window after it, minus what the critic expected, standardized to spread 1 within the update. Only the entry actually played gets a label. The other entries at that decision get none.

**Why that is weaker than it sounds:** about 98% of that advantage is shared by every decision of the same player-day. So within one day, a good move and a bad move carry nearly the same label. The label does not say which of the day's decisions caused the outcome.

**Where action-level information then comes from:** only from averaging across many days and games. The head sees features of the played entry (its type, the move or travel pair vector, whether it was NK2's choice). If days where a certain kind of entry was played end better on average than days where it was not, the head learns a positive number for that kind of entry. This is the usual way a value-of-action head is trained from noisy returns.

**What this can and cannot learn:**
- It can learn regularities that hold across many games, such as "leaving NK2's choice for this kind of travel tends to cost share". The follow coin helps here: whether we follow or deviate is random at each decision with a known chance, so that comparison is close to a controlled experiment.
- It cannot learn that one specific move on one specific day was the mistake. Other decisions of the same day confound it, and that only washes out with a lot of data.
- If two kinds of entry are almost always played on the same days, it cannot separate them.

**What the readings so far say:** the head explains 0.2 to 0.3% of the label's variance on fresh rows after two updates. That is the right sign and far too early to judge. If it stays near zero after 50 or more updates, the labels are too coarse for this approach.

The stronger alternative would be a label that differs between decisions of the same day, meaning credit on a decision's own step. You set step credit aside on 2026-11-09, so I have not built on it.

[2026-11-11 16:00] USER: no, I do no t understand, taking total share of value after 2 days is noisy but safe because we do not give a positive reward to everything, doing it at the end of each day is a bit riskier, looking for the change on every pickup is dangurous because it will learn to be too greedy. Do you look at actual change in value now after every pickup?

[2026-11-11 16:00] AI: No. Nothing looks at the value change after a pickup.

- **The head's label is the policy's own advantage, unchanged.** In the code the head's loss is its prediction minus `batch["advantage"]`, the same number the policy term uses in the same update. I added no new credit signal.
- **That advantage is the windowed credit you already approved:** share change over the days after the decision, with the critic's expectation subtracted. It is not measured at the decision's own step.
- **Step credit stays off.** The code for credit on a decision's own step has been commented out since your 2026-11-09 decision, and nothing today touched it.

So the head cannot learn greed from pickups, because it never sees a per-pickup reward. A pickup that looks good now and costs share over the following days gets the same label as everything else that day: the days-later result.

The only thing the head adds is averaging. The policy has to find a direction inside one update's games; the head keeps accumulating the same windowed labels across all updates.

My earlier phrase "what happened after the entry was played" was misleading. It meant the windowed share change after that decision, not an immediate change.

[2026-11-11 16:02] USER: so it learns "does picking up a like actions a good idea"?

[2026-11-11 16:02] AI: Yes, with one addition: it learns "is an action like this one, in a situation like this one, a good idea".

- **"Like this one"** means what the head can see about the played entry: its action type, the vector for the hero and target tile or area (for moves and travel), and whether it was NK2's choice.
- **"In a situation like this one"** comes from the same vectors, which carry the game state. It can learn that walking to a guarded mine is good with a strong army and bad with a weak one, as long as that difference is visible in the vector.
- **"A good idea"** means our share over the following days came out above what the critic expected, averaged over every time such an action was played.

So it is a statistical judgement about kinds of actions, not a verdict on one specific pickup. It needs many games before the average means anything, and it is a correlation: if a kind of action tends to be played on days that go well for other reasons, the head will credit it anyway.

The cleanest thing it can learn is the follow question, "does leaving NK2's choice here tend to pay", because whether we follow is decided by a coin at each decision.

[2026-11-11 16:03] USER: are we playing now and 90% of are actions are replaced with NK2 in current games?

[2026-11-11 16:03] AI: Yes. In every game the run plays now, training and eval, about 90% of our adventure-map choices are NK2's.

- **How it works:** at each turn decision NK2's planner says what it would do. The model then plays that with probability 0.9 and samples our own policy with probability 0.1. In the live run we end up on NK2's choice at 92% of decisions, since our own policy sometimes picks the same thing.
- **Where it applies:** every decision where NK2's choice can be expressed as one of our actions, which is 92 to 99% of turn decisions. For the rest we play our own policy.
- **What is still ours:** all battles (the battle model), plus the 10% of map decisions.
- **Training games:** these are self-play, so both sides play this way.

So the eval of 0.753 is mostly NK2's map play combined with our battles, against plain NK2. It is not evidence that our own map policy improved. The same checkpoint with following off scores about 0.51.

This is what I deployed as "get rid of the teacher, keep its insights": NK2 no longer trains our policy through a loss, but it now makes most of the moves. Our own policy only gets better if it learns where leaving NK2's choice pays, and on followed decisions it currently learns about ten times slower than before. The advantage head is my attempt to fix that.

If that is not what you meant by keeping NK2's insights, say so. The follow chance is one setting on the run line; at 0 the model plays its own policy with NK2's view only as inputs, and the eval goes back to about 0.5.

[2026-11-11 16:06] USER: this can work, but it is also super risky in the sense that we will only learn to fix NK2 and not really learn good moves in general

[2026-11-11 16:06] AI: Agreed, and the risk is concrete in three ways:

- **Our policy only ever sees NK2's games.** 90% of the states come from NK2's play, so our own policy never practises a whole game. With following off it still scores about 0.51 and gets no training in the states its own play leads to.
- **It learns patches, not play.** The only thing rewarded is "leave NK2 here". Opening, expansion and army building are never learned because NK2 does them.
- **NK2 becomes a ceiling and a dependency.** We could end slightly above NK2, and only with NK2 running inside every game.

What I will do about it, unless you object:

1. **Track our own policy honestly.** Each PC eval also runs with following off, and that number is the one that counts as learning. The 0.75 gets reported as "with NK2 driving".
2. **Train part of the games with following off.** In a share of self-play games (I would start at half), NK2's own choice is hidden and our policy plays the whole game alone, with NK2's scores and plan still visible as inputs. Those games give our policy full-strength gradients on its own states. The other half stays at 0.9 and feeds the advantage head with good play to compare against.
3. **Never mix the two in one game.** A follow-off player against a 0.9 follower would be close to training against NK2, which you ruled out.

Point 2 needs a small game-side switch that hides only NK2's choice, not its whole view. The existing dropout switch hides everything, which is the wrong test.

The cost is that the headline eval will drop from 0.75 toward the middle, since half the training no longer leans on NK2. I think that is the right trade: the follow-off score rising is the only evidence that we are learning the game.

[2026-11-11 16:11] USER: so in both training and eval we will have games assissted and unassisted by NK2, won't it mess up the regression head? teach it to detect which game is of which kind?

[2026-11-11 16:11] AI: It will tell the two kinds apart, and that is fine. It should not mess the head up, with one small addition I am making.

**Why detecting the kind does no harm:**
- **No kind of game is "better" on average.** Training games are self-play and every player in a game is of the same kind. Shares are relative within the game, so both kinds average the same outcome. The head cannot earn anything by learning "assisted games go well".
- **The label already has the critic's expectation subtracted.** The critic sees whether NK2's choice is shown, so differences in level between the kinds go into the baseline, not into the head's label.
- **A constant offset per kind cancels.** When the policy later reads the head, only differences between the options at one decision matter.

**Why the head should know the kind:** "is this move a good idea" depends on who plays the rest of the game. In an assisted game NK2 mostly plays the follow-up; in an unassisted game our own policy does. Those are two different questions, and the head can answer both only if it knows which game it is in.

**The addition:** the head reads the trunk's vectors, and the trunk may not yet encode clearly whether a choice is shown, because those input weights started at zero and learn slowly. So I am giving the head a direct flag for it, a separate per-action-type term for decisions with no NK2 choice. Otherwise it would average the two kinds together for a while.

**What could still go wrong:**
- The label is standardized over all rows of an update together. If unassisted games are much more volatile, their rows dominate the head's loss.
- The "does following pay" term only learns from assisted games. That is correct, but it has half the data now.

The head's fit is logged separately for the two kinds, so either problem will show.

**Evals:** the head is not trained on eval games, so the split eval cannot affect it.

- Our MOVE table has no "own tile" target, so there is nothing to map it to. Walking onto a teleporter from next to it already works as an ordinary move, which would explain why our own policy rarely hits this and following hits it at 5.5%.

**The fix I would build**
1. **One new legal entry: the hero's own tile in the MOVE table**, legal only when the hero stands on a usable teleporter. The centre cell of the window already exists in the table and is masked today, so this needs no new table and probably no schema change.
2. **The exit choice goes to the question head**, which already answers game dialogs. Where there is one exit, there is no question.
3. **What the entry is worth:** the model must see what is on the other side, or the entry is unusable (your rule on features). I would give it the value and travel time of the best area beyond the exit, in the same bounded form the travel entries use, and the "exit not seen yet" flag we already have for unexplored ones.
4. **NK2's request then maps to this entry**, so following and the inputs cover it too.

**What I would not do**
- Not a separate "teleport" action type. It would start with no prior and no data, and the move table already has the right slot.
- Not a mapping of NK2's request to "walk to the far side". We cannot path there without the teleport, which is the whole problem.

[2026-11-11 16:40] AI: Agreed on dropping it: no model change for aggression monitoring. On your question I checked the code, and the answer is partly different from what you assume.

**What is in the model today**
- **The battle forecast is fed to the move decision as explicit numbers.** Since 2026-11-04, each window tile carries the predicted chance that a monster there attacks, the chance we win, and the share of the hero's stake lost. MOVE reads them detached, so the policy's loss cannot bend the forecast.
- **So the policy is not left to dig the result out of a shared hidden state.** Your noise concern would apply to that design, and it is not the one we have.
- **Rule-based strength estimates are fed too:** our army against theirs, and a "hopeless" flag with a fixed −3 weight.

**Where I think the real issue is**
- **The forecast enters through weights that start at zero and learn at the policy's rate.** I measured today that such weights barely move: the fight weights are at about 0.005 after 3,000 updates, and the only fight term with real effect is the fixed hopeless rule. The model knows what will happen in a battle and makes almost no use of it.
- **The forecast is given as raw parts, not in the form a decision needs.** Win chance and stake lost say nothing by themselves until multiplied by what is at stake and what is gained.
- **Coverage:** the per-tile heads are described as covering wandering monsters. I have not traced today whether fights against heroes and towns get the same forecast or only the rule-based estimate.

**How I would model it better**
- **Give the fight's expected value directly, as a prior on the tile's logit:** win chance times what the fight gains, minus the expected stake lost, in the same share-of-empire unit and the same squashing the other priors use.
- **Start it at a fixed size with a known sign, with a bounded learnable correction,** like the other prior-anchored values. It then works from the first update and does not wait for a zero weight to grow.
- **It is exactly zero on tiles with no fight,** so it adds no noise to non-battle moves.
- **The advantage head reads the same number,** so "attacks like this end badly" can be learned in terms of the forecast.

This follows the two rules you already set: give features in the combined form the decision uses, and put known values in as a fixed prior plus corrections.

**Before building:** a check under 10 minutes on recorded games of how much the MOVE probabilities change when the forecast is flipped from "we win" to "we lose" on a tile. [2026-11-11 16:43] AI: Yes: the term is multiplied by "will there be a battle there", and tiles with no possible fight get an exact zero.

**The form I have in mind**

value on a tile = (chance a fight starts there) × (win chance × gain − expected stake lost × stake)

**Where "chance a fight starts" comes from**
- **A hard gate from the engine.** The game rules say whether stepping on a tile can start a fight: the tile holds an enemy, or it lies in a monster's guard zone. We already compute this. Where it says no, the term is exactly 0, with no learned number involved.
- **A learned probability on top, only where the gate is open.** A monster may attack, offer to join, or flee. The existing head predicts which, so the gate becomes a probability there.

**Zero has two meanings, so the model gets a flag too**
- "No fight possible here" and "a fight here is break-even" would both read as 0. The "a fight starts here" flag already exists as a separate input and stays, so the two cases remain distinguishable.

**Tiles where we lack information**
- **Enemy army not fully visible:** the forecast head already receives how detailed our knowledge is. I would not invent a number there; the rule-based strength estimate and the hopeless rule keep covering it, as today.
- **Unexplored tiles:** these are not move targets in the first place, apart from flagged teleporter exits, so the question does not arise for them.

One thing I have not verified is whether the learned forecast covers fights against enemy heroes and towns or only wandering monsters. If it covers only monsters, the term would use the rule-based estimate for the others until the head is extended.

[2026-11-11 16:45] AI: It should apply to all of them, and I agree zero is not automatically the right neutral value. Below is each auxiliary prediction, what it should feed, and what "not triggered" should mean.

I verified in the code that the per-tile battle heads are read by MOVE and that the plan forecast is fed back. The "read by the policy today" entries for the others come from the file's own description and are not traced.

| Prediction | About | Read by the policy today | Should feed | Neutral when not triggered |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per-tile battle: attack chance, win chance, stake lost | one option (a tile) | Yes, detached, through zero-start weights | that tile's MOVE logit, as expected value | 0 with the engine's "no fight here" gate. Reasonable. |
| Move consequences: battle score, change of each part of our empire value | one option (the tile played) | No | that tile's MOVE logit, as predicted change in value | 0 change. Reasonable, because it is a change and not a level. |
| Answer consequences (same, per option of a game question) | one option | No, as far as I can tell | that option's logit in the question head only | 0 change. Reasonable. |
| Hero still ours tomorrow | a hero's state | No | that hero's token, and the night-danger prior | **Not 0.** A survival chance of 0 means "dead". It must be fed as risk of loss, so 0 means safe. |
| Hero's army tomorrow against now | a hero's state | No | that hero's token | 0 as a log ratio means no change. Reasonable. |
| End-of-day value and tomorrow's resources against now | the whole turn | No | probably nothing | 0 as a log ratio. But it is a small critic and says nothing about which action is better. |
| NK2's plan per hero | a hero and area | Yes, fed back since today | hero tokens and travel entries | It has an explicit "no task" class. Reasonable. |
| Advantage head | one option | From deploy 59 | that option's logit | 0 means an average choice. Reasonable. |
| Value, growth and end heads | the state | No, credit only | nothing; they are the baseline | Not applicable. |

**The rules I would apply to all of them:**

1. **Only predictions about one option attach to that option's logit.** A forecast about the state (hero in danger, resources tomorrow) cannot say which action is better. It belongs on the hero or global token as information.
2. **Pick the unit so that "nothing happens" is zero.** Feed a change and not a level, a risk and not a survival chance, a log ratio and not a ratio. Then an untriggered or untrained prediction is harmless.
3. **Gate by the trigger when the engine knows it.** No fight possible means exactly zero, with a separate flag so zero is not confused with break-even.
4. **Read detached, and wire each prediction only to the head it concerns.** The policy's loss must not bend the forecast, and the answer forecast must not leak into move decisions.
5. **Start with a fixed sign and size where the direction is known,** with a bounded correction. A zero-start weight goes unused for weeks at our learning rate.

**One trade-off that is yours to make:** today these losses also shape the shared trunk, which is the indirect, noisy path you described. Externalizing adds a clean path but does not remove that one. Removing it would mean detaching the auxiliary heads from the trunk, which also throws away what the trunk learns from them. I would keep the trunk shaping for now and add the explicit paths, then compare.

The two rows I would build first are the per-tile battle value and the move consequences, since they concern the most frequent decision. The hero-survival row needs the unit fix before anything reads it.
